title: Work-order-type recipe (v1)
description: Schema for `.tera/work-order-types/<name>.hcl` recipes per PRD-012 §4.3 / ADR-045 §Part 5. Mirrors `pkg/workorder/registry.TypeBlock` plus the file-level `version` dispatch attribute.

name.description: Bare WO type name (the HCL block label). The loader namespaces it as <vault-id>/work-order-types/<name>.

description.description: Human-readable description surfaced in operator UIs.

based_on.description: The work-order type this recipe derives from, by its qualified name <vault>/work-order-types/<name> (ADR-147 D8). The resolved type is the base with this recipe's top-level attributes and blocks substituted in whole: replace, never merge, so a list is not appended, a block is not merged field by field, and declaring any block of a repeatable type (one claim, say) replaces every block of that type in the base. What this recipe omits is the base's, so the recipe slot may be omitted, or declared once to replace the base's with the same variant ending the same way (equal result_call and interactive). The base's contract is locked: a recipe declaring based_on may not declare input_schema, output_schema, output_guard, postconditions, decomposition, checkpoints, in_dispatch, subject, about_input, hitl_delegate_subject_input or tags, nor any connection block: whose credential the work uses for each connection is the base's, inherited exactly (ADR-148 D3). One level: a type declaring based_on cannot itself be a base. The base must be one this recipe's vault may read, and the merged type is validated as a standalone type, where every vault's contribution is composed, so an edit to the base reaches this type with no edit here.

previous_names.description: The qualified names this type was formerly registered under, each <vault>/work-order-types/<name> as based_on takes it, for a type moved between vaults or renamed (ADR-145 D7 Amendment 1). A Work Order stores the canonical name it was filed under, so the trains filed before a move keep the old name, which no longer names a registered type. Listing that name claims those trains: this type's own history block, its window and its archive, governs them, and a list of this type by its leaf or its name finds them too. Once the old name is gone, the claim also answers for the Work Orders still pinned to it: their in_dispatch verbs and claim {} requirements are read from this type (ADR-105 D2's 2026-10-15 amendment), so naming the old type here is how a replacement takes over its running work without stranding it. A Work Order filed under the old name after it is gone, at any door, is filed as this type, and its log records the follow as a type.followed event (ADR-145 D7 Amendment 2), so a train whose pinned instructions write the old name keeps filing children. A claimed name carries no policy of its own. A claim is held inert, and its trains kept whole as an unclaimed name's are, while the name is still a registered type, which governs its own trains, or while more than one type claims it; the history sweep reports an inert claim. KEEP THE ENTRY until no train stored under the old name remains in the hot store: removing it earlier returns those trains to being kept whole, and a train that ran a dispatch can be held by the step-binding gate for about 30 days whatever its window. A type declaring based_on never inherits its base's list.

tags.description: Labels every Work Order committed under this type carries, IN ADDITION to whatever its caller supplied (ADR-111 D1). The declaration goes on the TYPE because the type is the only place that knows what is true of EVERY instance: a caller knows about one Work Order and a worker knows about a queue, while the type is the unit over which "all of these are about a repository" is a well-formed claim. It is the opposite of description beside it, which describes the TYPE to an operator reading a catalog and does not reach an instance. A value is either a literal (lifecycle:implementation) or a reference to the Work Order's own inputs written as a ${inputs.X} template (repo:${inputs.repo_name}) — THE SAME SPELLING, SEMANTICS AND IMPLEMENTATION defaults.concurrency_key has used since before this attribute existed, reused rather than re-invented because a third substitution syntax beside ${inputs.X} and input_map's CEL is the failure those two are already documented as warning about. DELIBERATELY ANEMIC: field reference only, no function calls, no arithmetic, no conditionals, no nesting, and the answer to "I need the repo name lowercased" is a different input rather than a richer template, because an expression surface published on a recipe kind is append-only forever. A template is carried through the load UNEVALUATED — the inputs it reads do not exist while a config file is being read — and is materialised once, at the transition that COMMITS a Work Order to existing as work (ADR-111 D3): work_order.create for a Work Order filed directly, and work_order.release for a draft, never at draft-create, because a draft's inputs are editable right up to that moment. The derived tags are stored FIRST, in declaration order, then the caller's in the order supplied, with any string already present dropped (D7) — an order clients may rely on. A reference that does not resolve against the Work Order's inputs REFUSES the commit rather than emitting repo: or omitting the tag (D5), and a resolved value over 128 bytes refuses it too (D6). Once committed the tags cannot be removed, because work_order.edit is draft-only and derivation happens after the last edit (D8). tera does not interpret a tag's structure — it does not split on :, model a namespace, or detect a caller-supplied tag colliding with a derived one (ADR-111 D10). An element that is not a string literal or a ${...} template — a number, a function call, a %{...} directive, a nested list — is a load error naming its index, because a tag tera silently dropped reads exactly like one it kept; a value that is not a list at all, an explicit null for the whole attribute included, is refused naming the attribute rather than an index, because there is no element to point at. A TEMPLATE ROOTED AT ANYTHING BUT inputs — ${var.X}, ${env.X}, ${outputs.X} — is a load error naming the tag's index and the root that was written: inputs is the only name bound when a tag is materialized, so any other root refuses every work_order.create under the type rather than some of them, and tera config plan says so before anything runs. A var. reference the vault CAN resolve never reaches that rule, because variables are substituted into literals before a recipe is decoded; what it catches is the one nothing else does — a root that is legal in every other recipe attribute and meaningless in this one. A TEMPLATE REFERENCING AN INPUT THE TYPE'S OWN input_schema POSITIVELY DECLARES AS AN OBJECT OR AN ARRAY is a load error too, naming the input and its declared type (ADR-111 D6): a tag is a string, the type already carries the schema that says this input is not one, so tera config plan refuses it before anything runs rather than letting every commit of the type fail at evaluation. That check refuses only what is CERTAINLY wrong — a union (["string", "null"]), a property with no type keyword at all, a type keyword tera does not recognise, and a type declaring no input_schema at all are each left alone rather than guessed at, and a deeper traversal (${inputs.report.title}) interpolates the field rather than the object so the object's declared type says nothing about it. A template referencing an input the schema does NOT list as required is a WARNING and not a refusal: it silently makes that input effectively required, because an unresolvable reference refuses the commit (D5) and a tag template has no try() to coalesce it away — which is a legitimate thing for a type author to want, so the plan says so and lets it through. A repeated tag and an empty one are NOT refused here: deduplication is a property of the union at commit, and a length bound is declared elsewhere, so refusing either here would be a second rule that agrees with the first until the day it did not. Default: empty, and tags = [] is legal and says the same thing as omitting the attribute.

activity_partition.description: The ADR-113 activity partition every dispatch of this type resolves to: the scope deciding who may WATCH a run of this type live, and who may read what it did. It is the HIGHEST rank in ADR-113 D3's precedence — work-order type, then listener, then worker — and the reason is that the type is what the work IS rather than who happens to run it, plus ADR-105 D1's pin: a Work Order is pinned to its type's configuration for life, so a partition inherited from the type is as immutable as the pin and a run cannot change which team may read it by being re-dispatched under a different worker. Overriding is SILENT — with a total order over distinct kinds there is no disagreement to refuse, only a rank to apply — which is why the value a dispatch actually resolved to is recorded on the dispatch and projected back rather than left to be inferred; an operator who set a partition on the worker and had it beaten by the type would otherwise debug an ACCESS FAILURE against a value that never applied, because the grant they wrote names the partition they thought they had. UNSET IS AN ABSENCE AND NOT A DEFAULT: a type that declares none leaves the decision to a lower rank, and a dispatch nothing declares one for anywhere emits nothing, publishes nothing and stores nothing (ADR-113 D2). There is deliberately no fallback partition and no permissive default (ADR-075 D11) — routing undeclared invocations to an operator-only partition so nothing is lost is a permissive default wearing a conservative hat, and it is refused by ruling rather than by omission. The value names a partition an activity_partition recipe declares; that recipe is where the value's shape is refused offline (no /, no topic wildcard, no {principal} anywhere in it, and no leading _, which the topic grammar reserves for its own sentinels), and nothing here re-decides it. A value naming a partition no recipe declares is not refused here either: it resolves, and nothing is granted on it, which is the same end state as declaring nothing.

input_schema.description: Raw JSON Schema for inputs (heredoc body in HCL).

output_schema.description: Raw JSON Schema for outputs — the single authority on what done looks like for work of this type, which work_order.complete validates the result against. Compiled at load, so a malformed one fails while you are reading the file that holds it. IT MUST BE SELF-CONTAINED: an internal reference (#/$defs/...) is fine, and any $ref the compiler would have to fetch or read off the daemon's disk is refused, because the recipe is the declaration and a definition of done whose meaning lives in a second file is one no vault carries, no config plan diffs and no reviewer sees.

agent.description: REFUSED at load by name (ADR-136 D5 row 3; D11 removed the agent recipe kind): the daemon runs no model, so a type naming an agent recipe does not register — the vault loader degrades that type alone, and bootstrap HCL fails to load. Nothing inside the block is parsed. The member stays in this schema because the recipes contract's published level carries it (ADR-143 D3); the refusal, not a decode error, is what an author meets. The replacement is a capability or select work-order type dispatching at a harness, or a workflow whose only judgment is a capability step; the migration pointer is the section 'Migrating off the agent shape' in examples/code-lifecycle-types/README.md.

name.description: REFUSED at load by name (ADR-136 D5 row 3, D11): the agent recipe the refused type names (the HCL block label).

workflow.description: Dispatch this type to an authored workflow. The block label names the workflow. Exactly one of the workflow, capability, external or select blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4), or at most one when based_on is declared.

name.description: Authored workflow this type dispatches to (the HCL block label).

capability.description: Dispatch this type straight at a capability, without an authored workflow — sugar the wiring layer lowers into a one-step workflow (ADR-081 D6). The block label names the capability. Exactly one of the workflow, capability, external or select blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4), or at most one when based_on is declared.

name.description: Capability this type invokes (the HCL block label).

operation.description: Capability operation name. Required on this recipe — a capability recipe with no operation is refused at load.

input_map.description: How this dispatch's invocation params are built out of the Work Order's inputs, each value a CEL expression evaluated at dispatch. Omit it and the Work Order's inputs object is handed to the capability VERBATIM, key for key, which is what every capability recipe did before this attribute existed — so a type whose inputs are already shaped like the capability's params needs none. It exists because ADR-081 D6 calls this block sugar the wiring layer lowers into a one-step workflow, and without it the sugar was strictly less capable than its own desugaring: an authored one-step workflow can map its inputs onto a capability's params and the shorthand for exactly that could not. The lowering copies it onto the synthesized producer step, so the step and the type share one implementation and one meaning. The vocabulary is the workflow step's: input.<name> reads the Work Order's inputs, and a composite input is available as one — input.phases is a list of objects, so input.phases.map(p, p.name).join(", ") is an ordinary expression here. TWO SUBSTITUTION SYNTAXES LIVE IN THIS BLOCK AND THEY ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE: config interpolates ${inputs.X} against the Work Order's spec inputs, this maps input.X in CEL, a ${...} written here fails to decode, and declaring an input_map does NOT rewrite what config's ${inputs.X} substitutes against — the two are independent channels three lines apart. format() is not a serializer: "%s".format([input.phases]) emits cel-go's debug rendering of a composite, which looks like JSON and is not, and there is no JSON encoder in this environment — a recipe that wants a particular string composes it. An expression that cannot resolve fails the dispatch rather than substituting empty, which is the same posture config's ${inputs.X} takes. The steps namespace is refused at load: a capability recipe lowers to a workflow whose producer is the FIRST step, so no step has run when this is evaluated, and a mapping that genuinely needs another step's output wants an authored workflow recipe instead. On a recipe that declares attended {} it also reads parent, the Work Order the session was opened for, evaluated at the first dispatch (ADR-179 D5): null when it was opened for none, and otherwise parent.id, parent.type, parent.instructions (an off-tera item's instructions as rendered at its commit, and any other Work Order's body) and parent.off_tera. Everywhere else parent is refused at load. Default: unset, and the dispatch is byte-identical to one authored before this attribute existed.

config_map.description: Typed CEL expressions contributing binding configuration. Expressions see original input and completed steps only; null omits a key, and keys must be disjoint from config (ADR-131 D8).

result_call.description: Whether a dispatch of this type ENDS BY CALLING the submit verb on the reserved in-dispatch surface, with the whole ending record as typed arguments, instead of leaving a file behind for the daemon to read after the producer is gone (ADR-099 Amendment 4). The verb's input schema IS this type's output_schema, so the contract arrives as machine-read schema rather than as prose a recipe author transcribed, and a record that does not satisfy it is REFUSED BACK TO THE PRODUCER WHILE IT IS STILL ALIVE — an ordinary tool error naming the pointer, the constraint and the schema path, which it corrects and calls again. That is the whole reason to prefer it: the file mechanism evaluates the schema at work_order.complete, after the step has settled, so the refusal is computed at the one moment there is nobody left to hand it to. BECAUSE IT IS A TOOL'S INPUT SCHEMA, output_schema UNDER result_call MUST DECLARE type object AT ITS ROOT AND NO ROOT allOf, anyOf OR oneOf, and a type that breaks this is REFUSED AT LOAD — at tera config validate, at config apply and at the daemon's own load — naming the file, the line and the keyword: MCP requires an object input schema and model tool-calling APIs refuse a root combinator, so a client would drop the verb and every run would finish with no way to report; hoist a lone if/then to the root, and use dependentSchemas or a combinator nested under properties for the rest. It is the ONLY ending a type declares, and declaring it is optional: a type that omits it ends however its capability ends, which is what most of a deployment's types do. DECLARING IT BESIDE interactive IS REFUSED AT THE SAME THREE SURFACES, and for a different reason: ADR-129 D2's turn boundary IS the result file — an adapter yields a turn by leaving the pre-work marker in place and replacing it with a contentless suspending declaration — and a type that ends with the call writes no such document, so an interactive dispatch of one would end the conversation at its first turn or park at an inbox nothing recorded. The refusal names both declarations and both lines and spells both repairs, because either can be the one you meant to delete. The adapters refuse the same pair at dispatch with their own ending_unsupported code, and that refusal stays: a load surface cannot see a binding that acquires interactive from somewhere the recipe does not state. IT IS A SIBLING OF operation AND NOT A KEY INSIDE config, and the distinction is the substance rather than the filing: config is the handler-facing class, forwarded verbatim into the sandbox and described by the tool's config_schema, while an ending is daemon-read and runtime-facing, so the dispatched program neither has to understand it nor gets to disagree with it. It is per binding rather than per tool, because the same adapter is dispatched by types that end differently and a declaration on the tool would move an ending for producers that never agreed to it. THE DECLARATION IS PINNED, so a run ends by the mechanism it was pinned to at its first dispatch for its entire life (ADR-105 D1): migrating a type while one of its runs is in flight changes what runs NEXT and never moves the ending out from under work already dispatched. READ THIS BEFORE OPTING A TYPE IN: RETIRING THE FILE RETIRES THE CORPSE. ADR-091 dispatch salvage reads a result file left in the workspace by a session that died before reporting, and a dispatch offered the submit verb writes none. What remains is the session corpus in the dispatch's activity partition, which holds the attempted call — AND A PARTITION THAT DECLARES NO retention BLOCK KEEPS NOTHING ON DISK, so a deployment that opts a type into the call while running an unretained partition has no evidence path at all. See docs/ops/workorder-salvage.md and docs/ops/activity-and-the-session-corpus.md. Default: false, and the dispatch is byte-identical to one built before this attribute existed.

config.description: Binding config this recipe hands its tool as the invocation's binding_config — the same channel a workflow capability step's config uses, so the tool handler cannot tell which authoring surface configured it (ADR-082 D1). This is what lets a type invoke a tool with a required config_schema with nothing else in the loop to supply it. It sits inside the capability block because on the other recipes the config is either authorable somewhere that names the tool it configures — a workflow's capability step — or meaningless, as it is on an external recipe that dispatches nothing. String values may reference ${inputs.X} and are substituted against the Work Order's spec inputs at dispatch; a reference that cannot resolve is an error, not an empty string. A value that wants a LITERAL ${...} writes HCL's own escape, $${...}, and the escape survives the substitution — it reaches the tool as ${...} rather than being read back as the template the author escaped it not to be. VALIDATED AT LOAD AGAINST THE NAMED TOOL'S config_schema when that tool is declared in this configuration: the tool's config_defaults are composed beneath this block, as the dispatch composes them, and a recipe that cannot satisfy the schema — a required field missing, a key the schema does not admit — is refused at tera validate, tera config validate, config apply and the daemon's own load (where a vault recipe is degraded), naming the tool and the field, rather than loading usable and failing every dispatch. A ${inputs.X} value and a config_map key count as present and their values are not judged, because both are known only per dispatch. A capability no tool recipe in this configuration declares — a runtime-registered tool, a connector, an MCP projection — is not judged, and the dispatch-time validation stays its only check.

interactive.description: Whether a dispatch of this type is a CONVERSATION rather than a single run (ADR-129 D9). An interactive dispatch ends each turn by SUSPENDING RATHER THAN COMPLETING: the adapter writes a contentless suspending declaration, the run parks at paused:awaiting-interactive-turn carrying neither a question nor a predicate, and it sits at an inbox until somebody sends it a message, one of its own children settles, or the pause's deadline arrives — and everything that arrived while it was parked drains into the NEXT dispatch, in arrival order. IT IS A SIBLING OF operation AND NOT A KEY INSIDE config, and the distinction is the substance rather than the filing: config is the handler-facing class, forwarded verbatim into the sandbox and described by the tool's config_schema, while this is DAEMON-READ and runtime-facing in the sense a tool's mcp_servers block already is — resolved outside the sandbox, so the dispatched program neither has to understand it nor gets to disagree with it. THE BINDING MUST OFFER WHAT THIS REQUESTS: the tool's in_flight { yields_turn = true } is the offer, and a type declaring this against a binding that does not offer it is REFUSED AT LOAD — at tera config validate, at config apply and at the daemon's own load — naming both files and both lines. The refusal is the point rather than a strictness: a dispatch that quietly ran one-shot instead would be discovered by a person whose chat ended after one message. IT CANNOT BE DECLARED BESIDE result_call, and the pair is REFUSED AT LOAD at the same three surfaces, naming both declarations and both lines: a turn boundary IS a result file, and a type that ends by calling the submit verb writes none, so every dispatch of such a type would end the conversation at its first turn or park at an inbox nothing recorded. IT IS ALSO AN INPUT TO PAUSE DERIVATION, so awaiting-interactive-turn is derived for a type that asked for it and for no other, which is what keeps ADR-086's a type reaches the pauses it can honour, and nothing else true rather than handing every capability type a state it will never enter. Default: false, and the dispatch is byte-identical to one built before this attribute existed.

attended.description: Whether a dispatch of this type is ATTENDED: one process in a terminal its person attaches to, rather than a run nobody watches or a turn at an inbox (ADR-179 D2). IT IS A SIBLING OF operation AND NOT A KEY INSIDE config, for interactive's reason: it is daemon-read and runtime-facing. AT MOST ONE OF interactive AND attended: they are two answers to one question, what drives this dispatch — an inbox of messages, or a person at a terminal — and a recipe declaring both is refused at load. THE BINDING MUST OFFER WHAT THIS REQUESTS: the tool's attendable = true is the offer, and a type declaring this against a tool that does not offer it is REFUSED AT LOAD — at tera config validate, at config apply and at the daemon's own load — naming both files. AN ATTENDED SITE ENDS BY THE SESSION'S OWN SUBMIT CALL, so result_call = true beside it is refused as a second spelling of the same fact; an output_schema is admitted, and is that verb's input schema. The request and the offer are frozen into the configuration pin. Default: absent, and the dispatch is byte-identical to one built before this block existed.

unsandboxed.description: Whether the attended session runs as the host's user, outside the dispatch sandbox (ADR-179 D8). Default: false, the sandboxed session. TRUE LOADS ONLY UNDER THE KERNEL SWITCH attended_allow_unsandboxed (ADR-179 D14 item 1), a top-level bool in the bootstrap HCL that is false under every deployment_profile: while it is off, a type declaring unsandboxed = true is refused naming the switch, in one sentence, at the daemon's load, at reload, at tera config validate and at tera config plan, and a plugin carrying such a type is refused at plan. The switch is kernel-only and restart-only, so no vault edit turns it on; tera config validate reads no kernel and judges with it off. A Work Order pinned while the switch was on and dispatched or resumed after a restart with it off is held, not dispatched. Carried through the grammar, the lowering and the configuration pin.

host.description: The runner the attended session is placed on (ADR-179 D2, D7). It may reference ${inputs.X}; it is kept as written at load and rendered once, when a Work Order of this type is committed. An optional input that is absent leaves the field absent, and the session is then placed by the worker's pools like any dispatch. A reference to an input this type's input_schema does not declare is refused at load, as is a reference rooted at anything but inputs.

external.description: Declare that nothing in tera executes this type: something outside tera runs the work and the Work Order is tera's durable record of it (ADR-090 D2, ADR-139 D1). Which executor is exactly one nested block — mcp_upstream {} for a task on a registered MCP upstream, or off_tera { requirements, instructions } for work a taker outside tera picks up. Such a Work Order never enters the deps to deferred to capacity to dispatch gate chain, consumes no LLM-account seat and no worker concurrency slot, and is moved only by what tracks its executor. It takes no label because what identifies the executing party — which upstream and which foreign task id, or who took the work — is per Work Order and lives on the Work Order, not on the type. Blocks that describe a dispatch are refused on this recipe rather than silently doing nothing: volumes and environments are provisioned at a dispatch that never happens, postcondition check blocks lower into a synthesized workflow that is never synthesized, and an in_dispatch verb is offered to a run that never exists (its empty form stays legal, like postconditions none). Exactly one of the agent, workflow, capability or external blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4), or at most one when based_on is declared.

mcp_upstream.description: The work runs as a task on a registered MCP upstream serving the tasks extension, and that upstream's own feed moves the Work Order (ADR-090 D8). It takes no label and no fields: which upstream and which foreign task are per-Work-Order facts carried on the Work Order, so every wrapper in a deployment is an instance of one type. Exactly one executor block must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

off_tera.description: The work is picked up off tera's board by a taker outside tera, which reports on it (ADR-139). It takes no label, because what takes it is per Work Order rather than a resource this configuration declares. Exactly one executor block must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

requirements.description: What a taker must have to take this work — access, tooling, a checkout. It may reference ${inputs.X}; the text is kept as written at load and rendered once, when a Work Order of this type is committed — a live create or create_child, a composite-plan child, or the release of a draft — onto the Work Order's spec, the way tags are (ADR-111 D2/D3). A reference rooted anywhere but inputs, or to an input the input_schema declares as an object or an array, is refused at load and at config plan; one to an input the schema leaves optional warns, because a reference the Work Order's inputs cannot resolve refuses the commit rather than rendering empty. Optional. The type's description says what the work is; this says who can do it.

instructions.description: What a taker is asked to do. It may reference ${inputs.X}, under the same rules as requirements: kept as written at load, rendered once onto the Work Order's spec when it is committed, refused at load for a reference tags would be refused for, and refusing the commit when the inputs cannot resolve it. Optional.

lends_subject_to.description: The child types, by bare name in this type's own vault, that a Work Order of this type lends its delegation subject to (ADR-135 D4 Amendment 1). A child beneath off-tera work otherwise takes its filer's own subject, so a plugin holding work for a person as itself files children that act on nobody's behalf, and a child type binding a connection with filer {} is refused no_delegation_subject. A child of a type named here inherits the person instead, and records the parent as lent_by, when all of these hold: it is filed by the parent's current taker acting as itself; that taker is the plugin the person filed or released the parent through; and the parent has not ended — a child filed after it ends is refused. It is not impersonation: the person consented by filing or releasing the work through that plugin, and the loan reaches only the types named here. The list is copied onto the Work Order when it is committed, so a later edit of this type lends nothing more to work already filed. A name with a /, an empty or padded name and a repeat are refused at load. Optional; absent lends nothing. tera config plan and the plugin's install review show each loan.

select.description: Dispatch this type to one of a closed set of interchangeable candidates, chosen at admission from the Work Order's own input rather than at authoring (ADR-130 D7). Conditions precede all acquisition, and a candidate is selected only after its complete governed resource set has been acquired. It takes no label because it names more than one capability: the references are the candidate blocks' own capability labels. Exactly one of the agent, workflow, capability, external or select blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4), or at most one when based_on is declared.

input_schema.description: Raw JSON Schema for the SHARED input contract every candidate presents (heredoc body in HCL). It is not this type's own input_schema, which may additionally carry selection parameters such as an engine field the request reads. A site must declare at least one of input_schema and output_schema: the shared contract is what makes a candidate set interchangeable, and a site declaring neither asserts nothing its candidates must agree on.

output_schema.description: Raw JSON Schema the selected candidate's mapped result is validated against before anything downstream reads it (heredoc body in HCL). The candidate's own native output is validated against its native schema first, then translated by that candidate's output_map, then checked here.

request.description: CEL expression returning the candidate label this Work Order asks for, or null to leave the choice to the policy. It sees the Work Order's original input and, in the workflow spelling, the outputs of steps that have already completed. An explicit request never falls back: an unknown label, a value of the wrong type, an empty string or an evaluation error each refuse the admission rather than selecting something else, and a request naming a candidate whose capacity is exhausted waits for that candidate. Omit it to let the policy decide every time.

input_map.description: How the shared input is built out of the Work Order's inputs, each value a CEL expression evaluated once per admission and validated against input_schema before any candidate is visited. This is the direct form's equivalent of a workflow step's own input_map block, which the workflow spelling uses instead. An absent map and an authored empty one are different contracts and are digested differently.

policy.description: What decides when request is absent or returns null. A site always declares one, because an explicit request may be null and the policy is what answers then.

fixed.description: Name one candidate as the default. An open choice then behaves exactly as an explicit request for that candidate: it waits for that candidate's capacity and does not downgrade to another. Exactly one of the fixed or first_available blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

candidate.description: The declared label this site defaults to. Required on this variant — declared optional here so an empty one is refused by name rather than as a raw missing-argument diagnostic — and it must name a declared candidate.

first_available.description: Ordered automatic selection: the first candidate in the declared order that is eligible AND whose complete governed resource set can be acquired. Exactly one of the fixed or first_available blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

order.description: The preference sequence. It must enumerate EACH declared candidate EXACTLY ONCE: an omission and a duplicate both refuse, so adding a candidate without adding it here leaves the policy incomplete rather than silently ranking the new one last.

config.description: Binding configuration every candidate receives, whichever is selected. It composes with a candidate's own config only on DISJOINT keys: a key declared at both layers refuses rather than silently replacing the shared instruction. Only a tool's own config_defaults may be overridden.

config_map.description: Typed CEL expressions contributing shared binding configuration, under the same disjointness rule as config beside it (ADR-131 D8). Expressions see the original input and completed steps only; null omits a key.

candidate.description: The closed candidate set, in authored order. Referencing a candidate is not authority to invoke an arbitrary capability whose name arrived in user input: the set is fixed at authoring and a request may name only a member of it. Declaration order is NOT a preference source — an ordered policy enumerates the preference explicitly.

label.description: This candidate's site-local name (the HCL block label) — the value a request expression returns and an ordered policy enumerates. It is local to this execution site and is not a new global resource.

capability.description: The existing capability this candidate binds, by name, with the operation inside it. Required on every candidate.

name.description: The capability this candidate invokes (the HCL block label).

operation.description: The capability operation. REQUIRED on a select candidate — there is no invoke default here, unlike on a fixed capability step, because the native-schema gate is stated about the candidate's selected operation and a default would bind an operation nobody wrote into a contract whose point is that it was checked. Declared optional here so a missing one is refused in the select compiler's own words.

input_map.description: Translates the validated shared input into this candidate's native arguments. Its one root namespace is shared_input: it never names the raw Work Order input or another step. On a site that declares attended {} it also reads parent, the Work Order the session was opened for (ADR-179 D5), with the fields and null the capability recipe's input_map gives it; the site's common input_map does not. ABSENT and AUTHORED-EMPTY differ — an absent map means identity in this direction, which is what makes structural schema matching between the shared and native contracts mandatory there, while an empty one constructs an empty object.

output_map.description: Translates this candidate's validated native result into the shared output. Its one root namespace is native_output. Absent and authored-empty read exactly as they do for input_map.

config.description: This candidate's own static binding configuration. It composes with the site's config only on DISJOINT keys: a duplicate refuses rather than silently replacing the shared instruction.

config_map.description: This candidate's dynamic binding configuration, under the same disjointness rule as config beside it. A provider-specific model override at a selecting site requires an explicit request for that candidate.

interactive.description: Whether a dispatch of this site is a CONVERSATION rather than a single run (ADR-129 D9) — the same request the fixed capability recipe's interactive makes, declared ONCE ON THE SITE and NEVER ON A CANDIDATE. Being interactive changes the site's OUTPUT CONTRACT, since an interactive dispatch's declaration is contentless, and ADR-130 D1 requires every candidate to present one contract — so a per-candidate flag would let first-available selection change the contract by falling back, and candidate {} therefore carries no such attribute at all. THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THE OFFER SIDE IS THAT EVERY CANDIDATE'S BINDING MUST DECLARE in_flight { yields_turn = true }: a candidate whose tool does not is refused at load, naming the type file and line, the candidate label and the tool file. THERE IS NO MIXED SITE. The offer is frozen onto each pinned candidate, so a tool edit withdrawing yields_turn changes what runs next and does not change a conversation already pinned (ADR-105 D1). Default: false, and the dispatch is byte-identical to one built before this attribute existed.

attended.description: Whether a dispatch of this site is ATTENDED (ADR-179 D2) — the same request the fixed capability recipe's attended makes, declared ONCE ON THE SITE and NEVER ON A CANDIDATE, for interactive's reason: it changes the site's contract, and first-available selection must not change the contract by falling back. EVERY CANDIDATE'S TOOL MUST DECLARE attendable = true: a candidate whose tool does not is refused at load, naming the type file and line, the candidate label and the tool file. AT MOST ONE OF interactive AND attended. The offer is frozen onto each pinned candidate (ADR-105 D1). Default: absent.

unsandboxed.description: Whether the attended session runs as the host's user, outside the dispatch sandbox (ADR-179 D8). Default: false, the sandboxed session. TRUE LOADS ONLY UNDER THE KERNEL SWITCH attended_allow_unsandboxed (ADR-179 D14 item 1), a top-level bool in the bootstrap HCL that is false under every deployment_profile: while it is off, a type declaring unsandboxed = true is refused naming the switch, in one sentence, at the daemon's load, at reload, at tera config validate and at tera config plan, and a plugin carrying such a type is refused at plan. The switch is kernel-only and restart-only, so no vault edit turns it on; tera config validate reads no kernel and judges with it off. A Work Order pinned while the switch was on and dispatched or resumed after a restart with it off is held, not dispatched. Carried through the grammar, the lowering and the configuration pin.

host.description: The runner the attended session is placed on (ADR-179 D2, D7). It may reference ${inputs.X}; it is kept as written at load and rendered once, when a Work Order of this type is committed. An optional input that is absent leaves the field absent, and the session is then placed by the worker's pools like any dispatch. A reference to an input this type's input_schema does not declare is refused at load, as is a reference rooted at anything but inputs.

output_guard.description: CEL expression evaluated against outputs at completion. A false result moves the WO to paused:awaiting-review.

defaults.description: Retry, backoff, and concurrency defaults for new WOs of this type.

max_retries.description: Maximum retry attempts for a failed WO.

concurrency_key.description: HCL template that materialises a concurrency-key string when the Work Order is committed to execution: at create for one filed live, at release for a draft, so an edited draft commits the key its final inputs produce. A concurrency_key stated on the create or the draft itself wins over this template. May reference inputs.foo.

concurrency_max_waiting.description: How many Work Orders of this type may WAIT on one worker behind a held concurrency_key (ADR-045 Part 4, Amendment 2026-09-29). Setting it claims that instances sharing a resolved key are interchangeable while they wait, so a newer one supersedes an older one — right for a type filed per event (a triage of a red main), wrong for one carrying unique work. The line is the never-dispatched Work Orders on the worker with the same key in blocked:waiting-on-capacity, whatever blocked them; holders and anything before the capacity gate are not in it. When an arrival would overflow the line while the key is held, one candidate — the line plus the arrival — is superseded: the lowest priority, and among equals the oldest by created_at. An evicted waiter ends superseded with superseded_by naming the arrival that displaced it; an arrival that is itself the victim ends superseded with superseded_by naming the key holder. The event carries reason concurrency-overflow and a detail naming the key, the bound, the holder and the arrival. 0 is first-come-first-served: an arrival while the key is held is superseded at once. Omit for an unbounded line. A retried run, or any Work Order that has ever been active, neither counts toward the bound nor can be evicted. Refused when negative and when the type declares no concurrency_key. Not a work_order.create parameter; the value applied is the arriving Work Order's type's, read live.

concurrency_key_on_park.description: Whether a parked Work Order of this type keeps its concurrency_key (ADR-045 Part 4, Amendment 2026-10-04). hold, the default, keeps it while the Work Order is parked: a run that stopped to ask has not stopped working on what its key names, and a sibling admitted while it waits is a second run on one resource. release hands it back while the Work Order is parked, so another Work Order sharing the key is admitted as though the parked one held nothing, and no line forms behind it. Its resume does NOT wait for the key: a woken run of a releasing type may run beside the one admitted while it was parked. Declare release only for a type whose instances are safe to run together once one has parked, and that may park for long — a gate that waits days for a person's review, whose newer instance must not wait behind it, and whose older instance acts only on what is still its own. Beside hold and release the engine applies a rule of its own, whatever the type declares (ADR-153 D5): a capacity park (paused:awaiting-capacity) holds no key when every refusal it recorded is wakeless, a cause only a configuration or fleet change ends, as the seat gate classifies it (seatgate.ClassifyWake). A capacity park with any waking refusal keeps its key under hold, and so does every other park under hold, a question park among them, unless the run moved into it straight from a park that had released its key. The resume of a park that released its key re-takes it in the store before it executes, and stays parked while a sibling holds it; a run that passed the re-take and is parked again is classified afresh. Read live off the parked Work Order's type, as concurrency_max_waiting is read off the arriving one's. Refused when the type declares no concurrency_key.

max_steps.description: Runaway ceiling on the model turns one dispatch of this type may run. The daemon runs no model loop and enforces nothing here itself (ADR-136): it resolves the value, pins it, and carries it on the capability invocations the Work Order dispatches, as the invocation context's step_ceiling, for a capability that runs a loop of its own to honour. Omit to take the daemon default (200); 0 means unbounded. A ceiling, not a budget — a healthy loop runs one to two orders of magnitude under it.

max_total_tokens.description: Runaway ceiling on the input+output tokens one dispatch of this type may consume. The daemon runs no model loop and enforces nothing here itself (ADR-136): it resolves the value, pins it, and carries it on the capability invocations the Work Order dispatches, as the invocation context's token_ceiling, for a capability that runs a loop of its own to honour. Omit to take the daemon default (5000000); 0 means unbounded.

priority.description: The priority a Work Order of this type is filed with when its filer states none (ADR-045, Amendment 2026-10-14). Any whole number, negative included; higher is offered a seat sooner in the capacity walk, which admits waiting work in priority-descending, then arrival-ascending order. Omitted, the type files at 0, as it always has. It is written onto the Work Order's spec.priority at create, on every door that files one — work_order.create, create_child, a workflow child step, each child of a composite plan, and the trigger and mint paths that file through create — so get, list, tree and prioritize read it as any other priority. A priority the filer states, 0 included, wins over it, and refile and retry keep the priority the Work Order already carries. A static integer, never a template over inputs, read off the type current at create: a hot-reload changes only Work Orders filed after it, and a draft carries it from its create, editable with edit and not re-applied at release. A type declaring based_on inherits it with the rest of its base's defaults block unless it declares a defaults block of its own. Declare it on a type that is a single point in a train's dependency chain — an orchestrator, a verification — whose wait for a seat behind ordinary work stalls everything filed beneath it.

may_pause_for.description: Narrows the pause reasons a run of this type may reach. Leave it out in the ordinary case: the permitted set is DERIVED from the recipe's own structure, and this attribute only subtracts from that set — a reason the structure cannot honour is refused at load rather than silently dropped (ADR-086, 2026-08-31 amendment). The derivation, by what the type's execution site keeps across a park: a type that runs locally — an agent, workflow, capability or select recipe — keeps its Work Order workspace (the implicit one, or a managed work_order volume it binds) or its step and conversation state, so every reason is honourable; a capability or select recipe whose volume bindings make its writable producer root something other than a managed work_order volume could resume into a directory with another lifetime, so only awaiting-review — reached once the run has finished — is derived for it; a type declaring external { mcp_upstream {} } executes nothing of tera's and parks only where a mirrored upstream report maps to a park, so it derives awaiting-input; and a type declaring external { off_tera { … } } executes nothing of tera's either, but its taker's result can park it on a question, on its children or on named Work Orders, so it derives awaiting-input, awaiting-children and awaiting-event. Some reasons narrow further wherever they cannot arise: awaiting-capacity needs a dispatch of tera's for a pool member to wall (ADR-092 D7), awaiting-credential needs a producer of tera's holding a credential of tera's to report dead (ADR-086, same amendment, over ADR-110 D5), awaiting-upstream needs a tool step of tera's for an upstream_transient code to ride on (ADR-086, 2026-09-22 amendment), and plugin-contract-moved needs a dispatch of tera's calling a plugin under its own per-dispatch identity (ADR-140 D14) — none of which an external type of either executor has — and awaiting-review on an external type of either executor needs an output_guard or a postconditions check that a result could be refuted by. awaiting-approval is never derived: it has no trigger and no state, so a run parked under it could not be reopened. awaiting-interactive-turn is derived for a type that declares its dispatch INTERACTIVE (ADR-129 D9, interactive = true on the capability or select site) and for no other: it has a state, a trigger and several doors, and the declaration is the input that derives it, so a type reaches ADR-129 D3's inbox by declaring it rather than by naming the reason here — naming it in this attribute without the declaration is refused as a widening, and an external type cannot declare it. THE TWO ARE DEFINED SIDE BY SIDE (ADR-129 D3) because input is a generic word and an idle interactive session is not awaiting input: awaiting-input is a producer that asked a specific question and is stuck until a person decides it, and awaiting-interactive-turn is a session that has yielded the turn and is waiting at its inbox for whatever comes next — a message, any of its own children settling, or the pause's own deadline. Write may_pause_for = [] to say that runs of this type park for nothing at all; the recognised vocabulary is awaiting-input, awaiting-event, awaiting-review, awaiting-children, awaiting-approval, awaiting-capacity, awaiting-credential, awaiting-interactive-turn, awaiting-upstream, plugin-contract-moved. PREFER never_pause_for WHEN YOU DO NEED TO NARROW. This attribute enumerates the reasons KEPT, which makes it a statement about the vocabulary as it stood when the line was written: every pause reason minted afterwards is subtracted by it, by an author who could not have considered it. A declaration whose omissions all postdate the newest reason it names earns a load-time advisory finding saying so and naming both repairs, and the subtraction stands until an operator decides which they meant — nothing is widened behind an author's back.

never_pause_for.description: Narrows the pause reasons a run of this type may reach by naming the reasons REMOVED — the same subtraction may_pause_for performs, written the other way round, and THE ONE TO REACH FOR when a narrowing is genuinely wanted. The permitted set is DERIVED from the recipe's own structure (ADR-086, 2026-08-31 amendment) and this attribute only ever removes from that set; it is the exclusion form that makes the difference, because it says nothing about the reasons it does not name, so a pause reason minted after the line was written stays derived instead of being silently withheld from a type whose structure grants it. That is the failure may_pause_for has and this attribute does not: an enumeration of permissions ages, an enumeration of exclusions does not. Declaring both attributes on one type is a load error rather than an intersection — they are two answers to one question, and a reader would have to reconcile them to know what the type does. Naming a reason the structure does not derive is deliberately NOT an error here, unlike the same name in may_pause_for: there it is a claim about what the type MAY do and is refused as a widening, while here it removes something already absent, which changes nothing today and keeps saying what the author meant if the recipe later grows the structure that would derive it. A misspelled reason IS an error, because an exclusion list that excludes nothing looks exactly like one that worked. An empty list removes nothing and is the same as omitting the attribute — unlike may_pause_for = [], which is the strongest available narrowing. The recognised vocabulary is awaiting-input, awaiting-event, awaiting-review, awaiting-children, awaiting-approval, awaiting-capacity, awaiting-credential, awaiting-interactive-turn, awaiting-upstream, plugin-contract-moved — of which awaiting-interactive-turn and awaiting-input are worth telling apart from the first (ADR-129 D3): awaiting-input is a producer that asked a specific question and is stuck until a person decides it, while awaiting-interactive-turn is an interactive session that has yielded the turn and is waiting at its inbox.

on_restart_missed.description: Behaviour when a scheduled restart was missed.

decomposition.description: Built-in decomposition strategy. composite-plan materialises children from a children-array outputs payload.

environments.description: Virtual Environments provisioned at WO dispatch with WO-scoped ownership (PRD-013 §11.1 / ADR-057 D4).

environment.description: Environment declarations, each a named provider substrate.

name.description: Environment name (HCL block label; per-recipe unique; becomes the bound-tool name prefix, e.g. router.tty_type).

type.description: Environment type — the provider that serves it (ADR-087 D5: the provider is the environment's type). pty is a real pseudo-terminal wrapping a program; softshell is a pure-Go in-process bash over the mounted volume; remote-desktop (preview, ADR-085 D0) attaches to an operator-declared device over RFB and drives it from pixels. The name is remote-desktop rather than desktop or vnc: desktop reads as the desktop this daemon runs on, which is the inverse of the deny-by-default posture, and vnc names the transport, which is a field on the endpoint declaration.

mounts.description: Labels of WO/session volumes mounted into the substrate, resolved against the recipe volume bindings at dispatch. Required for the softshell provider, whose shell jails a mounted volume and has no other substrate.

suspend_policy.description: What happens to the live substrate when the owning WO pauses (ADR-057 D8). Empty means the provider's default: tear_down for softshell (its helper is freed while the Work Order is parked; files on the volume survive, cwd and shell variables reset, ADR-175 D2), hold for every other type. Write hold on a softshell to keep the helper across a park.

config.description: Provider-specific configuration. Well-known PTY fields are modeled inline (ADR-057 D4); the software-shell provider's fields live under the software_shell sub-block. Each field is valid only under the provider it belongs to.

cwd.description: Working directory: a mount label or an absolute path inside a mount. PTY only — the software shell presents the fixed virtual root /workspace (ADR-068 D8).

env.description: Create-time process env for the substrate. PTY only — the software shell runs under a pinned base environment, and a variable is set from the bash line with export.

bootstrap.description: Two-phase bootstrap (PRD-013 §7.2): durable provision-once, ephemeral startup-every. The software shell supports provision_once only (it has no live process to start).

provision_once.description: Commands run once when the durable volume is first provisioned.

expect.description: Declarative startup-expect step list (ADR-057 D10): no control flow, no eval. PTY only.

step.description: Ordered expect steps. The step wrapper is what preserves the authored order (ADR-087 Amendment 3): HCL decodes blocks into one slice per block type, so writing the variant blocks as bare siblings under expect would lose their sequence, and an expect dialogue is nothing but sequence.

match.description: Wait for a regex, then optionally type a reply. The block label is the regex. Exactly one of the match, send or sleep blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

pattern.description: Go regex to wait for (the HCL block label).

send.description: Literal or credential reference (keychain://, env://) typed once the pattern matches. A credential reference is resolved in the daemon and rides the FD-3 bootstrap frame; the plaintext never reaches the LLM transcript or any agent-visible surface.

timeout.description: Per-step ceiling on this wait (Go duration). Bounded above by the block-level overall timeout.

send.description: Type without waiting for anything first — rare but legal for unconditional prefixes. The block label is the value. Exactly one of the match, send or sleep blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

value.description: Literal or credential reference to type (the HCL block label). Same resolution and redaction path as a match block's send.

sleep.description: Pause unconditionally. The block label is the duration. Exactly one of the match, send or sleep blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

duration.description: Go duration to pause for (the HCL block label).

software_shell.description: Software-shell provider configuration (PRD-015 / ADR-067 D5, ADR-068 D6). Valid only under type = softshell; a recipe that sets it on any other provider is rejected.

external.description: Tier-2 allow-list: the command names that escape the in-process builtin tier and run as real sandboxed binaries. A name that is neither a builtin nor listed here hard-errors 127 — the shell never falls through to a real PATH. The ratified golden-path allow-list is git + go with network = true and no read_paths; see docs/ops/software-shell.md for the worked example, why gh is deliberately absent, and why the allow-list is documented rather than seeded.

name.description: Command name as typed on the bash line (the HCL block label), e.g. git. It is a bare command name, never a path: dispatch keys on argv[0] verbatim. A name a builtin already serves is rejected, since dispatch tries builtins first and the entry could never run.

path.description: Absolute host path of the binary to execute. Absolute is required rather than resolved: a relative argv[0] would resolve against the agent-writable workspace, turning an allow-list entry into run whatever the agent dropped under that name.

args.description: Fixed leading arguments prepended to whatever the shell line passed, so an entry can pin a subcommand or a flag.

network.description: Grant this external full kernel-level network access (Seatbelt network allows on macOS; Landlock TCP plus the seccomp address-family allow-list on Linux). Off by default and per-entry. There is NO domain scoping in v1: this is all-or-nothing. A future scoped mode would be an HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY domain allow-list, which is cooperative rather than containment — it constrains tools that honour those variables (git, curl, gh, go do), while a non-compliant binary can dial directly and non-HTTP protocols bypass it.

read_paths.description: Absolute host subtrees this binary may read, on top of the sandbox floor (ADR-069 D2 layer 2). Each entry grants recursive read and never write. Omit the attribute to attach the measured built-in default for a known command name (git, go, node, npm, curl); an explicitly empty list means floor-only. A relative entry is rejected at load time.

write_policy.description: Opt-in tightening of what the builtin tier may write inside the workspace jail (ADR-068 D6). Absent means permissive: the jail root is the only boundary.

allowed_subtrees.description: Restrict builtin-tier writes to these subtrees of the workspace. Empty means the whole workspace is writable. Entries are written the way the shell sees them: relative to the virtual root (src) or absolute under it (/workspace/src). An entry that cannot name a path under the virtual root is rejected — an allow-list that normalized away would otherwise read as no allow-list at all.

protected_paths.description: Deny builtin-tier writes to these paths and everything under them. Deny overrides allow. A destructive operation on an ancestor of a protected path is refused too, so renaming the parent cannot relocate protected content.

write_budget.description: Cap on builtin-tier write operations for the life of the session. 0 or unset means unlimited. A refused write spends nothing.

limits.description: Builtin-tier resource governors (ADR-067 D8), applied per builtin invocation. Absent means the built-in defaults.

sort_mem_budget.description: Bytes of input a bounded-memory builtin holds in memory before spilling a sorted run to scratch. Unset means the engine default.

scratch_bytes.description: Bytes of concurrently-live scratch one builtin invocation may hold in the spill area. Exceeding it fails the builtin loudly rather than filling the host disk.

max_record_len.description: Bytes of one line/record a builtin will read. Minimum 4096. Without it a memory budget is defeated by a single input with no newline.

merge_fan_in.description: How many scratch runs a bounded-memory builtin merges in one pass, and therefore how many scratch files it holds open at once. Minimum 2: a fan-in of 1 never reduces the run count.

endpoint.description: Name of the operator-declared remote_desktop_endpoint to attach to (ADR-085 D1). Required under type = remote-desktop and rejected under every other provider. A name and only ever a name: the host, port, transport and credential live in the operator's remote_desktop_endpoint declaration, and no attribute here can express them. Naming an endpoint is not reaching it — resolution is server-side and gated on the RBAC resource remote-desktop/endpoints/<name>/attach, deny-by-default.

geometry.description: Requested framebuffer size for a remote-desktop environment, as <width>x<height> (e.g. 1280x800). Valid only under type = remote-desktop; a PTY sizes its grid with cols/rows and a software shell has no screen. ADVISORY — the device decides (ADR-085 D1): the size the device announces at connect, and any mid-session DesktopSize change, is the truth, and every coordinate above the provider is in that space. v1's RFB transport cannot even ask (the client-side size request is the ExtendedDesktopSize extension, outside the ADR-085 D3 encoding set), so what setting this buys today is that a divergence between the request and the device's actual size is reported at attach rather than surfacing as coordinates that quietly do not match. Each axis must be in 1..65535, the range RFB's uint16 dimensions can express.

volumes.description: Volume bindings for this type's capability steps — the resource seam a workflow-recipe Work Order has no other way to declare (ADR-081 amendment). Type-level rather than step-level because the binding is per-Work-Order in lifetime. Bindings apply to capability steps only.

binding.description: Volume bindings, each keyed by a tool volume label.

label.description: Binding key matching a tool volume requirement. The label names the mount, not the volume: two holder-bound bindings that agree on provider, lifecycle, retention, ttl, share_key and config are one volume however differently they are labelled. same_as is how that sharing is declared, and a pair that would collapse without it is refused at recipe load — give one of them a source that differs if two volumes were meant.

type.description: Volume provider type, or references. Omit the attribute for an empty volume; a name outside this set is refused at recipe load, since nothing would serve it. git clones a repository into the mount; its config.repo is the repository's absolute URL (scheme://host/path), and a schemeless owner/repo is refused. github is a removed spelling: it stays in this enum because narrowing the enum would break the contract's append-only rule, and recipe validation refuses it, naming docs/ops/migrate-github-volume-provider-to-git.md (ADR-159 D10). hostpath borrows an existing host directory read-only without copying it, and is the provider to reach for when the mount is a repository checkout. corpus_view mounts the session corpus, narrowed to the partitions the requesting dispatch's own principal is authorized for, with a manifest naming what it was denied; it must be bound to the reader's own run (lifecycle = "work_order", and no_retention rather than ttl, since a view that outlived its run would describe a population that has moved on). references binds the volume to the Work Order's reference repositories (ADR-168 D2): repositories the work reads and never writes, each mounted read-only. Its config has one field, input, naming the input_schema property that carries the list; that property must be declared with "type": "array" and a "maxItems", and each item is held at filing to the platform's item schema (docs/reference/reference-repositories.md) whatever the property's own items say. A references binding may name connection, and declares none of lifecycle, ttl, retention, no_retention, share_key, same_as, when_input or credentials: its lifetime is the platform's and its commits are the Work Order's record. The tool volume it binds must be read-only.

lifecycle.description: Volume lifecycle policy. Dispositions are ephemeral (reclaimed by refcount) and persistent (explicit deletion). Holder kinds session, work_order and worker bind the volume to the requesting context; worker requires an explicit worker id and never falls back to the caller. Empty means ephemeral.

retention.description: Retain across the holder's runs until the deployment cap is exceeded, then retire the volume whole. The cap is deployment-owned, never a byte count on this binding. An alternative to ttl and no_retention; keep exactly one answer. Requires a holder-bound lifecycle and cannot be declared on a same_as alias. Retention is part of volume identity: different policies resolve separately.

ttl.description: Retention grace period (Go duration), refused at load if unparseable. On a holder-bound binding (session, work_order, worker) this is what selects ttl-after retention: the volume survives its holder's death for this long instead of being destroyed with it. Two bindings that agree on everything else and differ in ttl are two volumes, not one. One of the answers a holder-bound binding must give: declaring none of ttl, retention or no_retention is refused at recipe load, and docs/ops/upgrade-to-declared-retention.md is the migration for a deployment written before that rule. The exception is a provider that borrows its directory rather than provisioning one (hostpath): nothing ever destroys a borrowed directory, so no retention answer is demanded there — and a ttl declared anyway preserves nothing, it only holds the volume record and its quota count for the window.

no_retention.description: Explicit absence of retention, with the author's reason — an alternative to ttl or retention, and a way a holder-bound binding satisfies the discard rule. Say it when the volume holds nothing that exists only there: a toolchain cache, a scratch tree, anything regenerable. The volume is then destroyed with its holder, exactly as an undeclared one is today, so this changes no behaviour — it states the choice. The reason is mandatory and must be non-empty, following ADR-084 D6's posture for postconditions none: nothing here is worth keeping must read differently from nobody thought about it. Mutually exclusive with ttl and retention, since these are alternative answers. Rejected on a binding whose lifecycle binds no holder (ephemeral, persistent), where retention has no subject, and on a same_as alias, which takes its target's whole source. Accepted but not demanded on a hostpath binding, whose directory the daemon borrows and never removes — the answer cannot change anything there, so it is not asked for. Why the recipe must say it rather than the daemon defaulting it: a retained volume counts against the per-principal quota (ADR-084 D10), private scratch uses no retention while shared toolchain caches use worker-scoped bounded-by-size retention for exactly that reason, and nothing in a binding's shape distinguishes a workspace from a cache — only the author knows whether the directory holds work that exists nowhere else.

share_key.description: Deliberately share a volume within one holder and host: equal keys with equal provider, retention, ttl and config reuse one volume across invocations, even under different labels; different keys split contents. Never shares across workers or other holders. Omit to preserve existing keyless identity and paths. Cannot be declared on a same_as alias, which inherits its target's share_key. The recipe author must state this choice because only the author knows which bindings may share contents; the deployment still owns the cache byte cap. Matching concrete bindings in one block remain refused: use same_as for an alias or a distinct share_key for a split.

same_as.description: Bind to the same underlying volume as another binding label, and the way to declare that two labels in one binding block are one volume. The alias inherits its target's share_key and takes its target's whole source, so it may declare no type, lifecycle, retention, ttl, no_retention, share_key, config, credentials or connection of its own — one volume, and the target is the only binding that states its retention.

config.description: Provider-specific volume configuration. Free-form, and what is accepted depends entirely on type. The git provider reads repo — the repository's absolute URL (scheme://host/path); a schemeless owner/repo is refused — plus ref (a branch name, a tag name, or a FULL commit SHA — 40 hex digits, or 64 for a SHA-256 repository; unset means the remote's HEAD. A SHA checks the workspace out on a detached HEAD at that commit, so a session that pushes must create a branch first; an abbreviated SHA is not accepted and is treated as a branch name, which the remote refuses), sparse (a sparse-checkout path list), and the two ADR-128 object-donor attributes below. mirror selects the host's local git object mirror, and IT IS ON UNLESS YOU TURN IT OFF (ADR-128 D9): a git binding that names no mirror attribute borrows objects from the donor, so a clone transfers roughly the commits since the last fetch rather than the repository. mirror = false is the whole of the opt-out and restores the pre-ADR-128 clone byte for byte, --depth 1 included. THE COST OF LEAVING IT ON IS DISK AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE A RETAINED WORKSPACE FILLS ONE: a donated clone is dissociated, so it keeps no pointer to the donor and is a self-contained repository — which means it carries the whole packed history (133 MiB for kottera/kottera) into every retained workspace, where a shallow clone carried a fragment. D2 rules that trade acceptable on the ground that disk is the cheap resource and the uplink is the scarce one; a deployment for which that is false writes mirror = false. What it CANNOT change is what the clone checks out: the clone still contacts the real remote, still negotiates against it, and still ends at the ref the remote publishes, so a stale or missing donor costs bytes and never correctness (D1). max_age bounds how stale the donor may be before this provision fetches it (a Go duration, default 1h) and is a bandwidth dial for the same reason; it is refused beside mirror = false, where there is no donor for it to age. The store itself is daemon-owned and unnameable by design (D7) — a persistent volume resolves by binding label, and a nameable store would be a mountable one — so the recipe chooses whether to use it and nothing else; its size is the deployment's, at platform.git_mirror_store_cap on a daemon and git_mirror_store_cap in runner.hcl on a fleet host. EACH EXECUTING HOST KEEPS ITS OWN: the clone is performed by the machine that provisions the workspace, so a dispatch placed on a runner uses that runner's mirror and pays that host's first cold clone. Operator page: docs/ops/git-object-mirror.md.

credentials.description: Provider credential overrides for this volume.

connection.description: The connection a git binding clones and fetches with (ADR-148 D5), named by its .tera/connections/<name>.hcl stem. Whose credential it is comes from this type's own connection "<name>" { filer {} | worker {} } block, so a person's work clones as the person and a trigger's as the worker; a binding naming a connection the type chooses no holder for is refused at load and at config plan, naming it. The daemon resolves the holder's credential once at dispatch start and hands it to the git provider on the executing host, which clones outside the sandbox, so the credential never enters it; a holder who cannot use it parks the run before the workspace is created, and the clone never falls back to the worker's credential or to the host's git configuration. A references binding names a connection the same way, for the credential its references are read with; with none they are read anonymously, never with the host's own credential (ADR-168 D4). Refused beside credentials, which is a second source for the same credential, on a binding whose type is neither git nor references, and on a same_as alias, which takes its target's whole source.

when_input.description: Make this binding conditional on one Work Order input, named by its input_schema property. When the input is given the binding resolves as declared; when it is absent the label is an EMPTY volume with this binding's lifecycle, ttl, retention and share_key, and no config, credentials or connection — the dispatch still succeeds and the tool still gets its mount. Absent means the key is missing, JSON null, or the empty string: "" is what a blank form field or flag sends and no provider can provision from it (git refuses an empty repo), so reading it as given would only move the failure from this gate to the provider; every other value, false and 0 included, is given. It is also the opt-in to templating optional inputs: in a gated binding a config attribute (or list element) naming an input the Work Order did not supply is LEFT OUT, so the provider applies its own default — for git an omitted ref is the remote's HEAD. An ungated binding is unchanged: a ${inputs.X} naming a missing input fails the dispatch, and templating an input input_schema does not require is warned about at recipe load and at tera config plan. The two outcomes are distinct volumes (different provider), and the decision is made once per dispatch by the daemon before placement, from the pinned binding and the Work Order's unchanging inputs, so a dispatch on the daemon host and one on a fleet runner, and every park, resume and retry, see the same outcome. Refused naming an input input_schema does not declare (the label could never be anything but empty), naming a required input (it can never be absent), on an empty binding (both outcomes are already empty), and on a same_as alias, which follows its target's gate. Its absent outcome takes part in the same-volume check like any binding, so a gated binding whose empty outcome would equal a sibling's is refused there.

toolchains.description: Provisioned toolchain stores a dispatch of this type mounts read-only, by bare toolchain name (ADR-109 D14). THIS IS THE NORMAL HOME of a toolchain requirement, and the reason is a distinction only the type can draw: it knows what the WORK needs, so frontend work declares a browser and backend work on the same daemon, through the same tool, does not. The tool recipe is the second home and carries only what is true of the tool in EVERY dispatch — claude-code needs its harness, which is not a property of any particular work. A dispatch acquires the UNION of the two, with the TOOL'S ORDERED FIRST: the tool's requirements hold for every dispatch while the work's are the local addition, and that ordering is what makes the composed environment deterministic rather than a function of which declaration was read first. Within this list, DECLARATION ORDER DECIDES where each toolchain's environment contributions land — first-declared lands leftmost among the prepends and leftmost among the appends — so reordering the list reorders a composed PATH. A NAME AND NOTHING ELSE, because a consumer of a toolchain says only which: the store is deployment-wide, no invocation supplies a binding, and the definition owns the version key, the provisioning command and what the toolchain contributes to the environment. The name resolves in this type's own vault, else in the system vault (ADR-147 D6): a vault that declares the name gets its own definition for its own types, and a system-vault type always gets the system vault's. Another vault's toolchain is named qualified, <vault>/toolchains/<name>, and resolves only when that vault is granted share toolchains (invoke on vaults/share/toolchains); the reference is a dependency edge, so that vault cannot remove the toolchain while this type requires it, and a plan changing it names this type. The system vault's toolchains need no grant. Each vault's definition has its own store and lock entry, keyed <name>@<vault> outside the system vault. The name may not contain '@'. Refused on an external recipe, which nothing in tera executes and which therefore has no dispatch to mount a store into. A blank entry and a repeated one are load errors: the first mounts nothing while reading as a requirement, and the second reads as a second store when a store is mounted once however many times it is named. Default: empty, which mounts nothing — and a work-order type that does not declare a browser produces a dispatch with no browser, which is the half of the design that keeps backend work cheap.

hitl_delegate.description: ADR-079 D4 delegation policy for this type's Work Orders when they pause awaiting input, overriding the owning worker's. none refuses a delegate outright, assist confines it to its policy allow-list, auto lets it answer whatever it judges answerable. Empty inherits the worker.

hitl_delegate_subject_input.description: Names the input of THIS type that carries the subject Work Order id, marking the type as an ADR-079 D4 HITL delegate. At creation the subject's effective hitl_delegate is resolved and a none refuses the creation; the resolved policy is stamped onto the new Work Order's hitl_delegate input. Must be a required property of input_schema.

about_input.description: Names the input of THIS type that carries the id of the Work Order this type's work is ABOUT. The referent is a Work Order id and never a world subject — an input carrying a <kind>/<id> world subject is named by the separate subject block (ADR-100 D1), which is why this attribute is spelled after the about edge it derives rather than after the word subject. Naming one input from both is a load error: one operand cannot be both a Work Order id and a world subject. Declaring it makes work_order.create materialize an about relation from each new Work Order to the one that input names, so a general query for the work about a given Work Order finds this type's — which a per-type input alone cannot answer. The input stays an ordinary operand: it is schema-validated, may be required, and is read from CEL by the recipe; the edge is derived from it, so the two cannot disagree. The named property must be declared by input_schema and must not be declared as a non-string type, both checked at load. It need NOT be required — unlike hitl_delegate_subject_input, an absent or empty subject is a legitimate state (a sweep that names no single Work Order) and yields a Work Order with no edge rather than a refusal. A subject id that names no Work Order refuses the creation rather than producing a dangling edge. The derived edge is authorized by the CREATE grant alone (ADR-096 D6): it needs neither api/v1/workorders/relate nor reach on the subject, because the caller chose none of it — the relation is always about, no note is attachable, and the one degree of freedom is an operand the type already obliges it to supply. That is what keeps adding this attribute to a type from changing the grants its callers need, and it is why a cross-worker type may declare it.

subject.description: Which of THIS type's inputs carry a <kind>/<id> WORLD subject — what the work is about in the world, as against about_input's Work Order id (ADR-100 D1). Repeated: the block label names the input, and a type declares at most four.
