A creation reads each named input, parses the value as <kind>/<id>, and writes the binding to the subject index, so the Work Orders about a thing are findable FROM that thing rather than only by reading inputs back out of every row. The input stays an ordinary operand — schema-validated, may be required, read from CEL by the recipe — and the binding is derived from it, so the two cannot disagree; a template spelling (subjects = ["device/${inputs.device_id}"]) was rejected on exactly that ground, because a template is a second authored representation of one value that can be set in one place and forgotten in the other. Three states bind nothing and all three are legitimate: the type declares no block, the input is absent or null, and the input is the empty string (the shape a sweep takes when it names no particular thing). A present non-string value, a value that is not <kind>/<id>, a kind the deployment has not declared as a subject_kind recipe, and a kind outside this block's own kinds list each REFUSE the creation rather than producing a dangling binding. Authorization is the create grant alone (ADR-096 D6, ADR-101 D1): no separate relate resource and no reach check on the subject, because the caller chose none of it — which is what keeps adding a subject block to a type from changing the grants its callers need. A label naming a property input_schema does not declare is a load error, as is a label also named by about_input or hitl_delegate_subject_input, and as is a fifth block — the bound is four on both sides of a conjunctive match, because the index takes a row per (Work Order, subject) binding and work needing five simultaneous referents is work about a situation.

input.description: The input of this type that carries the subject (the HCL block label). Must be a declared property of input_schema, and must not also be named by about_input or hitl_delegate_subject_input — those carry a Work Order id, and ADR-100 D1 rules that a Work Order is never a subject under any kind.

kinds.description: Which subject kinds this input accepts, naming declared subject_kind recipes. OMITTING IT IS A DECISION, NOT A DEFAULT: without it the type accepts any kind the deployment declares, which is right for a sweep or an audit and a defect for a type that operates on one thing — recalibrate-sensor with no kinds accepts machine/4. Checked at load against the declared kind set, so a typo fails there rather than at the first creation that happens to hit it.

claim.description: Which subjects a dispatch of this type must HOLD before it runs (ADR-101 D2-D8) — as against the subject block beside it, which is what the work is ABOUT. A claim is a durable lease over a <kind>/<id> subject, held by a principal within a scope, and unlike an index binding it GATES: a Work Order requiring a subject somebody else holds does not dispatch, and blocks in blocked:capacity with a block_reason naming the subject, the holder and the holder's node. Repeated, and the block label names the requirement — a hard lockout on a machine and a soft claim on a test are two requirements rather than one. THREE AXES HAVE NO DEFAULT AND MUST BE WRITTEN: hardness, scope and on_park. hardness is the one ADR-101 D5 singles out and the reason is not style — it is the one place in the design where a wrong default is a physical-safety failure rather than an inconvenience, since a maintenance lockout that fails open because nobody typed the word is a machine that energises while someone is inside it, and a default would be SILENTLY wrong in the common direction because the case that dominates authoring instinct is soft. scope and on_park refuse a default for the same reason one rung down: each has two ways of being wrong that point in opposite directions, so neither has a conservative fallback to guess. A requirement names its subjects two ways and may mix them — subjects names them literally in ADR-100 D1's <kind>/<id> spelling, and subject_inputs names one of this type's own subject blocks so the claim is over whatever that operand carries at dispatch — with at most four across the two, because a requirement's set IS ADR-100 D3's conjunctive set and ADR-101 D6 acquires it in canonical <kind>/<id> order, all or nothing. DECLARATION ORDER IS THEREFORE NOT SIGNIFICANT, which is what stops two authors who never met writing two recipes that deadlock against each other. THE BLOCK HAS TWO HOMES AND THEY COMPOSE: this and the capability recipe, and unlike checkpoints, observations and in_dispatch the two are NOT selected between — a dispatch acquires the union — because a selection's failure mode here is a capability that declared a hard lockout being dispatched under a type that declared none, and running unclaimed. Refused on an EXTERNAL recipe: such a Work Order never enters the deps to deferred to capacity to dispatch gate chain, so the moment a claim is acquired never arrives, and an interlock that never acquires reads as containment while providing none. The ledger, the pre-dispatch gate, the scopes' release edges and the park behaviour have landed; the ADR-101 D8 TTL sweep is a separate item and NOTHING RENEWS, SWEEPS OR EXPIRES yet, so a claim comes back on the edge its scope or its on_park names and not on a clock.

name.description: This requirement's name (the HCL block label), unique within the recipe. It is how a refusal, a block_reason and an operator's read all name WHICH requirement, which is the only handle a recipe declaring two of them has.

subjects.description: Subjects this requirement is over, named LITERALLY in ADR-100 D1's <kind>/<id> spelling — machine/4, plant/line-3. The fixed-asset case, where nothing carries the referent as an operand: a trigger-fired sweep names the thing it sweeps. Each is parsed at load, and its kind is checked against the deployment's declared subject_kind recipes wherever the load can see them — the vault load can, and offline validation does not judge it rather than refusing a correct recipe on the strength of not having looked. A repeat is refused: acquiring one subject twice is not a stronger claim than acquiring it once, and a repeat cannot buy room under the bound. Combine with subject_inputs freely — the bound of four is over the two together, and at least one subject across them is required, since a requirement naming none acquires nothing while reading as an interlock.

subject_inputs.description: Subjects this requirement is over that arrive as OPERANDS, each naming one of this recipe's own subject "<input>" {} blocks. This is what lets a generic recipe lock the thing it was asked about — recalibrate-sensor locks the device its device_id input names — and it names the subject block rather than templating a value ("machine/${inputs.machine_id}") for ADR-100 D1's own reason: a template is a second authored representation of one value that can be set in one place and forgotten in the other, and the ADR-101 D1 index binding is already derived from that operand. One authored operand, two derived records, which cannot disagree. A name no subject block on this recipe declares is a load error listing the ones that are, because it would resolve to nothing at dispatch and a requirement that resolves to nothing is the interlock's fail-open direction. WHAT THAT DIRECTION COSTS AT DISPATCH IS THE GATE'S RULING RATHER THAN THIS BLOCK'S: ADR-100 D1 gives a subject input three states that legitimately bind nothing — absent, null and the empty string — and a hard requirement whose subject is one of them must REFUSE rather than proceed unclaimed.

hardness.description: REQUIRED, AND THE ONE AXIS IN THIS DESIGN THAT REFUSES A DEFAULT (ADR-101 D5). hard is containment: if the claim store cannot be reached the work REFUSES — it does not proceed, does not degrade to soft, and does not retry its way into proceeding — and the refusal says that this deployment could not establish whether the subject was held, not that it was. soft is advisory: the work PROCEEDS, and the fact that it proceeded unverified is RECORDED. Both halves of soft are the contract, because a soft claim that proceeded silently has discarded the only evidence that anything was unverified. A requirement omitting this FAILS TO LOAD, naming the file, the requirement and both repairs, and that refusal is the feature: a wrong default here is a physical-safety failure rather than an inconvenience — a maintenance lockout that fails open because nobody typed the word is a machine that energises while someone is inside it — and it would be SILENTLY wrong in the common direction, because the dev-queue case that dominates authoring instinct is soft. THE TWO HARDNESSES' BEHAVIOUR IS A SEPARATE ITEM; this attribute is parsed and refused today and governs nothing yet.

scope.description: REQUIRED, and the lifetime the claim is held for — which is to say what ENDS it (ADR-101 D4). dispatch releases when the invocation ends, the seat-shaped case, and is the only lifetime an invocation bound to no Work Order has. work_order releases when the Work Order reaches a terminal state. train is SELF PLUS DESCENDANTS-OF-SELF, adopting ADR-098 D2's ruled vocabulary rather than coining a second one — that phrase admits four readings and taking the ruled one keeps one meaning in the system — and an enclosing scope SATISFIES an inner requirement, so a parent holding machine/4 at train scope satisfies its descendants and they acquire nothing, without which a child deadlocks against its own parent. operator is held by a person with no dispatch behind it until they release it: the physical lockout-tagout case, where a technician takes machine/4 by hand before opening a guard and no Work Order models the hand inside the machine. NO DEFAULT, because the two ways of guessing wrong point in opposite directions — a claim scoped narrower than its hazard is an interlock that was not there when it mattered, and one scoped wider is a subject nobody else can take. THE RELEASE EDGES AND ENCLOSING SATISFACTION ARE A SEPARATE ITEM; this attribute is parsed and refused today and governs nothing yet.

on_park.description: REQUIRED, and whether the claim survives a park (ADR-101 D7). hold keeps it: a parked Work Order can sit for days awaiting a person, and for a machine mid-disassembly the hazard the lockout exists for is exactly what a park does not end. release gives it up: a flake fix whose operator went home leaves the subject idle while the work is not. NO DEFAULT, because the two fail in exactly opposite directions and neither is conservative in general — which is why ADR-101 makes this a per-requirement declaration rather than a platform rule. Note the one pause it does not govern: paused:children is distinguished from the operator-facing pauses and holds regardless, because a parent waiting on children it filed has not stopped working on the subject. IT GOVERNS AS OF WAVE 4 ITEM 11 of PLAN-2026-08-learned-operational-knowledge, in both directions and on all three acquirable scopes — a park hands back what declares release and keeps what declares hold, including at dispatch scope, because D7 makes the park behaviour a property of the requirement rather than of the scope's own release edge. A RESUME RE-TAKES WHAT THE PARK HANDED BACK, and if the subject was taken by somebody else meanwhile the resume is REFUSED rather than run uncovered: the Work Order goes back into the pause it held with its parked-run record and its workspace intact, a resume_refused event names the incumbent, and it resumes by itself once the subject comes back.

ttl.description: How long the claim is held before it expires, as a Go duration (ADR-101 D8). OMITTING IT IS A STATE RATHER THAN A DEFAULT: it declares NO CLOCK, and both halves of what a clock costs are real — a hard claim with no clock at all is how a plant acquires a lock nobody remembers taking, and a hard claim that auto-released on one would unlock a machine on a timer while someone is still inside it. D8's answer is that EXPIRY DOES NOT MEAN THE SAME THING FOR BOTH HARDNESSES, and that split is the safety property: a HARD claim's expiry ALARMS — the claim persists, the subject stays held, and it surfaces as overdue for a person to clear — while a SOFT claim's expiry RELEASES, because nobody's safety rests on it. A zero or negative duration is refused rather than read as either: it is not the same statement as no clock and cannot be honoured as one. Renewal is load-bearing here in a way it is not for a seat, because a work_order- or train-scoped claim is bounded by a Work Order rather than by one dispatch — for a coding session a two-hour sandbox timeout, and for a parked one under on_park = "hold" unbounded by anything but the operator. THE SWEEP, THE RENEWAL AND THE EXPIRY SPLIT ARE A SEPARATE ITEM; this attribute is parsed and refused today and governs nothing yet.

connection.description: Whose credential a dispatch of this type uses, per connection it uses (ADR-148 D3): the filer's (filer {}) or the worker's (worker {}). Repeated, one block per connection: the block label names a connection a .tera/connections/<name>.hcl recipe declares — the type's own plugin vault's when it carries the name, else the system vault's, and a type naming one no recipe declares is refused at load and at plan, naming the type and the connection. The choice is a fact about the work rather than about the harness or the CLI that carries it, so it is declared here and nowhere else: it governs every consumer in a dispatch that names the connection. A type that names no connection declares nothing here and resolves as if the block did not exist.

name.description: The connection (the HCL block label): the bare file stem of a .tera/connections/<name>.hcl recipe, with no vault or kind prefix. It binds the recipe's own release first: in a plugin vault carrying the stem, that installation's connection (plugin.<installation>/connections/<name>); otherwise the system vault's (ADR-159 D5.7). Or another installation's connection by its declared address, plugin.<plugin>/connections/<name>, resolved where the recipe loads through the writing vault's binding: a plugin's manifest builds_on, or a .tera/builds-on/<installation>.hcl declaration; a bare stem never names another installation's connection. A type names each connection once.

filer.description: Use the FILER'S credential for this connection: the delegation subject's own, the person on whose behalf the Work Order was filed (ADR-135 D4). Work with no delegation subject - filed by a trigger, a schedule, a mirror or the daemon - has no filer to act as. Takes no label and no fields: the person is a property of the Work Order, not something the recipe names.

worker.description: Use the WORKER'S credential for this connection: the one the owning worker binds in its own connection "<name>" { value = ... } block (ADR-148 D3). Takes no label and no fields: the binding is declared once, on the worker.

step_up.description: Which of this type's Work Order acts a PERSON must confirm with a step-up on tera's own page, and by which methods (ADR-173 D10). Repeated: the block label names the act, once per act. review is the review gate's three edges out of paused:awaiting-review (approve, reject, rework) as one authority; answer is an answer delivered out of paused:awaiting-input, and a wake that delivers none is not the act; submit_result is an off-tera taker's complete or failed declaration, and a paused one is not the act. The declaration is written onto the Work Order at the commit that makes it work (a live create, or the release of a draft) from the type current then, and moves only with a re-pin, which writes it again: a type that gains a step-up changes what is filed next, never what is already filed. Refused at load: an unknown act, a repeated act, submit_result on a type without external { off_tera {} }, and answer on a type declaring hitl_delegate = "auto". A type declaring based_on that declares any step_up block replaces its base's set in whole. The guard keys on the state machine's edge, so every door that fires a gated act meets it — work_order.transition, work_order.answer and work_order.submit_result, the management and kit invoke routes, the CLI, a parent or HITL delegate answering, and a correspondence reply — and it refuses the act unless it presents a step-up spent for that act on that Work Order and satisfied by a method the block accepts; a verb called without one begins a record and refuses step_up_required with the URL of the page the person confirms on.

act.description: The act a person must confirm (the HCL block label): review, answer or submit_result. Unique within the type.

methods.description: The methods a step-up for this act may be satisfied by (ADR-173 D9). Omit it for passkey only, the default. A declared set must include passkey, so every step-up can be satisfied by the strongest method; ["passkey", "email_code"] is the only other set, for an act a guest without a passkey performs. An empty, unknown or repeated entry is refused at load. passkey is a satisfying passkey with user verification whose anchor is not an email code; email_code is an act code mailed to the person, or a passkey registered in an email-code session.

label.description: This type's own words for the act, shown to the person on tera's step-up page and carried as label on the step_up_required challenge, so a plugin's own UI can show them before sending the person to the page (ADR-173 D10 Amendment 1): "Confirm your review of the Q3 guide". The page shows them as text, never markup, marked as the type's words, above tera's own line naming the act and the Work Order, which a label cannot replace or hide. Omit it to show the type's description there instead, made one line and cut to 200 characters; a type with neither shows tera's line alone. Plain text on one line, at most 200 characters; an empty label, or one containing a line break, another control character or a bidirectional formatting character, is refused at load. It is not a template: nothing is substituted into it. The words are read from the type as registered when the step-up is begun, while what is gated and by which methods stays the row's.

checkpoints.description: What work of this type reports WHILE IT RUNS (ADR-095 D6) — as distinct from what must be true of the request (input_schema), of the report (output_schema, output_guard) or of the world at the end (postconditions). The type owns this for Work-Order-bound work and that is a real choice: a general-purpose capability dispatched under a type has no way of knowing that this kind of work reaches a review stage and that kind does not, and the type does. The same declaration has a second home on the capability recipe for an invocation with no Work Order; the two are selected between and never merged, so a Work Order of this type whose type declares nothing refuses every checkpoint even where the dispatched capability declares a vocabulary of its own. Omitting the block and declaring phases = [] are both refusals and are deliberately distinguishable — the second says the author considered the question — and unlike postconditions, omitting it is NOT warned about: a type that declares no vocabulary has only declined to report progress, which is a legitimate answer for work short enough that a crash record buys nothing.

phases.description: The closed set of phases work of this type may report, in declaration order — the type author's own vocabulary, which is legitimately domain-specific: an implementation type reaches a phase a research type never does. Each is a KEY a consumer matches on rather than a label it prints, so whitespace and control characters are refused. A phase spelled other is refused by name: a catch-all inside a closed set is the free-text fallback the closed set exists to remove, since everything a producer would have narrated ends up under it. An empty list is legal and is the explicit statement that nothing here reports progress. Re-entering a phase is legal and expected — a retry genuinely re-enters the phase it failed in — and sequence numbers are monotonic, so the re-entry is visible as two records rather than one silently overwritten.

payload_schema.description: Raw JSON Schema for the domain payload — the half of a checkpoint the platform envelope has no field for (heredoc body in HCL). Omit it to declare none: a type that declares no payload schema REFUSES a checkpoint carrying a payload, because the schema is the prescription and a payload nothing prescribes records a shape no consumer can read. No permissive stand-in is inferred. Refused outright when phases is empty, where it could never be consulted. IT MUST BE SELF-CONTAINED: an internal reference (#/$defs/...) is fine, and any $ref the compiler would have to fetch or read off the daemon's disk is refused, because the recipe is the declaration and a schema whose meaning lives in a second file is one no vault carries, no config plan diffs and no reviewer sees. Write it as a prescription rather than a permission: a checkpoint answers what would I want to know if this died right now, not what is happening, so artifact identity earns a place and a percentage-complete does not.

postconditions.description: What must be true of the WORLD once a Work Order of this type reports complete (ADR-084 D1) — as distinct from what must be true of the request (input_schema) or of the report (output_schema, output_guard). Either a set of named check blocks, or the explicit form none = <reason>; the two are alternatives and declaring both is a load error. A type that declares no postconditions block at all is warned about rather than refused, and nothing is ever inferred from that silence. Checks are lowered into ordinary capability steps on a capability recipe's synthesized workflow and evaluated when the run finishes, so declaring one DOES change runtime behaviour: the verifier is invoked, the outcome routes per the policies below, and the Work Order will not complete on a refuted claim. Two things a deployment owes a type that declares checks: the named verifier capability must exist, and the owning worker must be granted it — work_order.create refuses a Work Order whose worker is not, so an unresourced check turns the type off rather than degrading quietly (ADR-084 D5). On an authored-workflow recipe they are refused outright, and none = <reason> stays legal there. Checks are also refused on a type that requests interactive turns (interactive = true on its capability or select recipe), because the pair cannot run: a check reads outputs.* that an interactive run never writes, the check steps are chained onto a producer step that conclude never advances past, and on_refuted = reinvoke cannot be served once the conversation has ended and the workspace is gone. That refusal is a not-yet rather than a decision against the combination, and none = <reason> stays legal beside the request.

none.description: Explicit absence, with the author's reason (ADR-084 D6). Use it when nothing about this kind of work is checkable — the ad-hoc claude-task type is the worked example, since work that states no kind states nothing to verify. The reason is mandatory and must be non-empty: the whole purpose of the form is that no postconditions because nothing applies reads differently from nobody thought about it. Mutually exclusive with check blocks.

max_feedback_attempts.description: Bound on judged re-invocation for this block (ADR-084 D9): how many times a refuted check may hand its feedback back to the producer before the Work Order goes to review. Defaults to 1. This is a separate budget from defaults.max_retries, which means mechanical re-dispatch of an identical input; the two do not multiply, and exhausting this one routes to review rather than to another mechanical retry. Only reachable when some check selects on_refuted = reinvoke.

check.description: The checks, each an ordinary capability invocation plus a CEL predicate over its result. A type declares any number: the world is correct for this kind of work is rarely one proposition. They run in declaration order with no short-circuit, their outcomes merge conjunctively, and the feedback of every refuted check is concatenated in the same order — so the order written here is the order an operator or a re-invoked producer reads.

name.description: Check name (the HCL block label), unique within the block. Every check is independently named because the verdict recorded on the Work Order keys on the name — which check refuted, at which attempt.

capability.description: Name of the capability that verifies the claim. An ordinary capability invoked the ordinary way, which is what makes verification inherit the per-step permission gate, the audit trail and the per-invocation telemetry. The deployment must grant it to the Work Order's worker; a type that declares a postcondition therefore names a capability its deployment has to resource.

operation.description: Operation on that capability, e.g. pr_state.

when.description: Optional CEL guard deciding whether this check runs at all, e.g. has(outputs.pr_url). It sees input (the Work Order's inputs), outputs (what the producer reported) and steps (earlier results), but NOT result — it decides whether the verifier is called, so it cannot see what the verifier returned. A false guard SKIPS the check, and skipped is not verified: it contributes nothing either way. Note the hazard the ADR names: a postcondition set in which every check skips has verified nothing while looking like it passed, which is a configuration defect rather than a clean bill of health.

input_map.description: How the verifier's parameters are built, each value a CEL expression. Carried verbatim by the loader and evaluated in the lowered step's environment at run time, so it can reference the Work Order's own vocabulary rather than anything known at config-load time.

verified.description: CEL predicate deciding whether the claim holds, e.g. result.merged == true. It sees result (the verifier's own result) on top of everything when sees. Required — a check with no predicate cannot resolve. Resolution order per ADR-084 D3: a step error, or a true indeterminate, means indeterminate; otherwise this expression decides between verified and refuted.

indeterminate.description: Optional CEL predicate over result meaning the check could not answer — a rate limit, an expired credential, or an eventual-consistency window (result.mergeable == null is the worked example, because GitHub computes mergeability asynchronously). It exists so a transport blip does not become a false accusation against a session that did its job: indeterminate never silently completes and never fails, it re-checks and then goes to review.

on_refuted.description: What happens when THIS check is refuted. review (the default) pauses the Work Order for a human; fail fails it outright, saying re-invocation is futile for this claim; reinvoke hands the feedback back to the producer for a bounded self-correction. Across several refuted checks the most conservative policy wins (fail > review > reinvoke), so reinvoke happens only when every refuted check opted into it. Empty means review — a type opts into self-correction rather than out of it. reinvoke re-enters the producer step with the rendered feedback and the structured verdict on its invocation envelope, bounded by this block's max_feedback_attempts (default 1) and enforced in the executor rather than in the policy; the checks re-run on the way back down, so the Work Order completes on the second verdict or — once the budget is spent — routes to review with every attempt's verdict on the record, never to another mechanical retry (ADR-084 D7/D9).

on_indeterminate.description: What happens when THIS check cannot answer — a transport failure, an expired credential, a rate limit, or an eventual-consistency window. review (the default) pauses the Work Order for a human once the bounded re-check below is spent; fail fails it; complete completes the Work Order anyway, the author's statement that this check is advisory. complete is the ONLY path to completing a Work Order on an indeterminate verdict and it must be written down — it is the one setting that re-opens the gap postconditions close, so it is never inherited, and across several indeterminate checks it applies only when every one of them selected it. reinvoke is deliberately not offered: an indeterminate has shown nothing to be wrong, so handing a producer feedback about it asks it to fix a claim nobody refuted.

max_retries.description: Bounded re-check for this check, lowered onto the verification step's own intra-dispatch retry budget (ADR-081 D8) rather than adding a second retry ladder. Default 0 — one attempt. Know what the step retry does and does not do before writing one: it re-attempts transport and tool errors only, and never re-evaluates the check's when or input_map. So this bounds the step-error road to indeterminate; it does NOT re-poll a verifier that answered successfully with an indeterminate-shaped result (a null mergeable stays null however many retries are budgeted). Composes multiplicatively with the Work Order retry ladder, exactly as a workflow step's max_retries does.

feedback.description: The message handed to a re-invoked producer, saying what is wrong and what would fix it. Written as a template over the Work Order's own vocabulary, so a $-brace interpolation is preserved verbatim at load and rendered at refutation — against input, outputs (what the producer reported), steps and result (what this verifier returned). Every refuted check's feedback is rendered and concatenated in declaration order so one re-invocation addresses everything at once, and the concatenation is recorded on the verdict whatever the policy: it is what an operator sent to review reads, not only what a re-invoked producer would be handed.

in_dispatch.description: What a RUNNING DISPATCH of this type may DO about its own train (ADR-098 D1) — file successors under it, read back what it filed, read the train it is itself part of, and unstick, repair, withdraw or commit the ones it filed directly — and, beside those verbs, which governed tools its session is handed on the same server, each with the binding config the type gives it (tool, ADR-153 D7). The fifth statement, beside the four about the request (input_schema), the report (output_schema, output_guard), the world at the end (postconditions) and what the work REPORTS while it runs (checkpoints). Its subject is the one none of those has: not what must be true, and not what is narrated, but what the run may DO. A sibling block rather than a section inside checkpoints, deliberately: that block has a second home on a tool recipe governing invocations bound to NO Work Order, and every verb here is Work-Order-bound by construction, so a section inside it would be silently inert in one of its two homes. It also has a different blast radius and a different reviewer — what a run reports and what it may do to its train are worth being separately readable. ONE VERB IS ON BY DEFAULT, and it is artifacts (ADR-098 Amendment 5): every type whose runs have a session is offered it whether or not it declares this block, because it is the run's own file inbox and outbox — it names no Work Order, its handles are train-scoped, its bounds are platform constants and no capability grant stands behind it — and a type that must not have it writes decline = ["artifacts"]. Otherwise omitting the block offers NOTHING and is the right default for nearly every type: a type that has not said what its runs may reach has authorized nothing, and no other permissive default is inferred (ADR-075 D11). Omitting it and declaring verbs = [] both refuse every verb that must be declared and are deliberately distinguishable — the second says the author considered the question — and neither declines artifacts. Unlike postconditions, omitting it is NOT warned about, because the warning would recommend a widening nobody asked for. Refused on an EXTERNAL recipe when it declares any verb or grants any tool, the same kind-affinity volumes and environments already have there (ADR-090 D2): a foreign executor runs that type's work and tera dispatches nothing, so there is no run to offer a verb to and no later wiring can produce one; verbs = [] stays legal, like postconditions none. Since ADR-098 WI-F2 the declaration is live rather than inert: a dispatch of this type is offered exactly the verbs declared here that this daemon can serve, and a verb the type did not declare is refused by name with the reason rather than reported as an unknown tool. The verbs are read live; the tool grant is pinned with the run (ADR-105 D1).

verbs.description: The acknowledge verb permanently accepts a failed:awaiting-ack outcome of a direct child and forecloses retry. The verbs a run of this type reaches about its OWN dispatch, its own children and the train it is part of, from a closed set whose members differ in what they REACH as much as in what they do. The reads and the write about its train: create_child files a successor Work Order under the running dispatch — the run's own decomposition, and the one verb here that files work; list enumerates the run's descendants; get reads one Work Order and tree reads a subtree. Their scope is SELF PLUS DESCENDANTS-OF-SELF and nothing else: a run reaches the Work Order it is running and the ones it filed, never an ancestor and never a sibling, because a run's descendants are a run's own doing while everything else is a read of work it did not file. TRAIN is the one read scoped wider (ADR-098 Amendment 3): it answers with the Work Orders in the train the run is PART OF, rooted at that train's root, so it reaches the run's ancestors, its siblings and everything beneath them. It takes NO ID — the train is derived from the running dispatch — so there is no spelling of it that reaches a train the run is not part of, and a supplied id is refused rather than ignored. Self is addressed by the ABSENCE of an id and never by passing one — get with no argument is the only admissible spelling, and get(id = <the run's own id>) is refused by name even though the answer would be identical, because parenthood and identity on this surface are facts the platform holds rather than parameters a producer supplies. The SINGULAR ACTING verbs are scoped one level tighter — the run's DIRECT CHILDREN, matching create_child's own scoping. The recovery verbs unstick a child (ADR-098 Amendment 1): answer answers a question a direct child asked, transition drives a direct child's review gate (approve, reject, rework — and only those three: answer, retry and cancel are their own verbs), and retry puts a direct child's failed:awaiting-ack dispatch back on the queue with guidance. This state is settled but not terminal; bare failed is acknowledged and requires a new Work Order instead of retry. Two of them govern a child that has not run yet: edit repairs one of the run's own DRAFTS in place — only the fields it states, keeping the Work Order's id so a sibling that depends on it still points at the thing that was fixed — and cancel WITHDRAWS one, which is create_child's inverse. Their boundaries are NOT the same and the difference is deliberate. edit reaches a draft and nothing else, because editing a released Work Order is unavailable anywhere to anyone (ADR-104 D5) and an edit to a child that may dispatch at any moment is racy in a way a withdrawal is not. cancel reaches a child that has never been handed to a dispatch: a draft the run has not released, AND one it released that is still scheduled or blocked — neither has executed anything, so withdrawing either classifies no outcome. What cancel still refuses, by name and with its own code, is a child that is running, one that has finished, and one that failed and is queued for a further attempt — the attempt behind that last one is an outcome whatever state the row now reads, and cancelling a dispatch that has run is a supervisor's judgement this surface does not offer at all. edit does not offer type (changing it changes what the Work Order IS), worker (a child's owner is the parent's, and create_child refuses to file one anywhere else) or relations (asserting a typed edge is operator-class), and each is refused by name rather than as an unknown field. Each of the five REQUIRES an id and none of them addresses self, because a run is not its own child. RELEASE (ADR-104 D6) has the same direct-child scope over a different subject: it commits drafts the run filed beneath itself out of draft and into the ordinary lifecycle, which is the second half of filing a breakdown for approval — file the children with draft = true, have the breakdown approved, then release the set. It takes a SET and applies it atomically, so a breakdown whose items depend on each other cannot end up half-committed; there is no singular spelling and no subtree flag, because a draft beneath one of the run's children is a grandchild and out of reach. RECALL (ADR-104 D3, amended 2026-10-01) is release's inverse over the same direct-child SET: it returns children the run released that have NEVER BEEN DISPATCHED to draft, keeping their ids, so a breakdown whose instruction changed after it was released can be repaired with edit and released again rather than cancelled and re-filed. A child that is running, has finished, or failed and is queued for another attempt is refused by name, as is one already in draft; one refused member recalls none of the set, and a reason is required because whoever is waiting on the work reads it. edit and cancel are singular for the opposite reason: repairing or withdrawing one item has no all-or-nothing property to lose. Nothing checks whether the run parked before releasing: the gate is the park a type's own contract obliges, not this grant, and the record reads park, answer, edit, release for anyone auditing it. The asymmetry is the decision: a run may SEE however deep its train goes and may ACT only one level down, so every level answers only its own children and responsibility follows the tree. A target inside the train that is not a direct child is refused with its own code, distinct from the out-of-train one, because it is in your train and it is yours to answer are different facts. ARTIFACTS (ADR-107 D1/D7, ADR-123 D9/D10) is scoped by neither of those rules and is the one verb here whose subject is a FILE. It publishes a file the run produced and hands back an opaque handle; it FETCHES a file another run in the same train published and gave the run the handle for, WRITING IT TO A PATH THE RUN NAMES rather than handing the bytes back in the answer — so a parent can settle did this render at all by opening the file with its own tools, which nothing else on this surface lets it do, since everything a run reports travels and everything it produces stops at the edge of its own storage; and it LISTS THE FILES WHOEVER FILED THIS WORK ORDER ATTACHED TO IT, which is the input direction of the same channel. THE FETCH IS WHY A 32 MiB INPUT COSTS NO CONTEXT: the answer is a path, a size and a digest, and the run opens as much of the file as its work needs. A fourth operation, read, hands the bytes back as content and is served only to a TOOL speaking the contract channel, which pays no context for them; it is withheld from the model-facing server on purpose, because that is the operation that spends a session's context on a file and ADR-107 D2 Amendment 1 exists to stop it being the default. ONE ENTRY GRANTS EVERY OPERATION, on transition's precedent, and the reason is structural rather than stylistic: the roles are per-call rather than per-type, since every non-leaf run in a train both publishes upward and reads downward within one dispatch, while a leaf granted only the read gains nothing. The attachment listing joins the same entry for that reason again — a run that may redeem a handle may list the handles it was itself handed, and no deployment wants one without the other. Two entries would have narrowed nothing real and would have made this the surface's first two-ended pair, with its ends declared on DIFFERENT work-order types and nothing able to check that they compose — create_child does not declare which types it files, so there is no type graph, and the failure would be the channel's own purpose inverted: a child publishes, the parent's read is refused as undeclared, and the parent escalates to a person. IT TAKES NO WORK ORDER ID ON ANY OPERATION: a published file is addressed by the handle publishing returned, which is random and carries no filename and no Work Order, so a reader is HANDED each one and nothing enumerates what a descendant PUBLISHED. The attachment listing takes no argument at all, which is what makes its scope structural rather than checked — there is no field in which to name a Work Order, so it is always the running dispatch's own, it never answers with an output of any Work Order including the run's own, and ADR-107's refusal of train-wide output browsing is untouched by it. What a run is told about its attachments arrives unbidden at dispatch besides, so the listing is what a session that lost that list calls rather than the only way to learn of one. NO ATTACHMENT IS MATERIALIZED INTO A WORKSPACE (ADR-123 D9): the handle and the platform's own invitation are the whole of what a run is given, at every size, and the bytes are pulled by presenting the handle to this same verb. The scope rule therefore lives in the handle rather than in this surface's reach checks — a handle is redeemable by any run in the TRAIN it was published in, which is one step wider than ancestors-only on purpose, because the case that decides it is a run relaying a handle to a sibling that verifies its work. The declared content type is validated WHEN THE FILE IS PUBLISHED, against what a reader could actually be shown, because the publisher is the party that can still fix it and is still running while a reader discovering it later holds a handle to bytes nobody can deliver. Size bounds and how long a published file survives are PLATFORM CONSTANTS rather than attributes of this block (ADR-107 D5): a recipe author does not know how much disk the deployment has, so a per-type cap is a knob nobody can answer. Publishing is offered HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE — an operator does not publish into a train. The spellings an author is likeliest to reach for are refused by name rather than as unknown words: create (parenthood self-asserted; use create_child), siblings (reading beside yourself is not a verb of its own; use train, which answers with the whole train and takes no id), publish and artifact_publish and artifact_read (the file channel is one grant rather than several; use artifacts), complete and fail (terminal classification belongs to the ending record, not to a mid-run call), force_fail (a supervisor's judgement about a dispatch, not a run's about itself), and pause and park (suspension is a declaration about how the dispatch ended, and a call here would be a second authority on that with the precedence rule invisible from both sides). ARTIFACTS IS THE ONE VERB OFFERED WITHOUT BEING LISTED HERE (ADR-098 Amendment 5): a type with a session gets it by default and turns it off with decline, so listing it is legal and redundant. An empty list is legal and is the explicit none of every verb that must be declared; it does not decline artifacts. none is not a member: write verbs = [] instead.

decline.description: The verbs this type turns OFF from the set every type with a session is offered by default (ADR-098 Amendment 5) — today only artifacts, the run's own file inbox and outbox. Absent declines nothing. A list of verb names beside verbs rather than a per-verb boolean, because an opt-out is a bare may-I with no second axis (docs/hcl-authoring-conventions.md section 9), and it is the ONE spelling of the opt-out: verbs = [] does not decline. A declined verb is never offered, a run reaching for it is refused naming this list, and an attach to a Work Order of this type — create --attach, deliver, interrupt, create_child — is REFUSED, consuming no handle, because a run of it could never read the file; the type read says so beside its in-dispatch surface. Refused at load: a verb that is not on by default (declining it would decline nothing), one also listed in verbs, and a duplicate. Legal on an EXTERNAL recipe, which is offered nothing either way. Like every in_dispatch statement it is read live rather than pinned, so a reload that adds it reaches the next dispatch of a Work Order already filed, and a derived type inherits its base's.

tool.description: The governed tools a dispatched SESSION of this type is handed, beside the verbs and on the same reserved tera server (ADR-153 D7). Repeated, one block per tool, labelled with the tool it grants: a native tool such as web-fetch, or a tool recipe as <vault>/tools/<stem> or its bare stem. Each is served under its LEAF (kb-read for plugin.kb/tools/kb-read), so a harness reaches it as it reaches a verb and no adapter learns anything. A type that grants no tool is offered none (ADR-075 D11). Refused at load: a tool no registry resolves; a name two tools answer, rather than choosing one; a config that fails the tool's config_schema; a tool declaring a writable volume, or any volume but a read-only tracked_checkout_input one, because a granted tool is handed its binding config and never the run's volume bindings; a leaf that is an in-dispatch verb (declared here or not), a name the reserved server already serves, or another granted tool's leaf, which is refused and never resolved by choosing one; and any tool on an EXTERNAL recipe, which has no session to hand it to (in_dispatch {} that grants none stays legal there). The grant is the type's half of the authority and never the whole of it: a call is admitted only when the dispatch's own worker also holds invoke on the tool under the spelling the label wrote, as a step of that worker's Work Orders naming the tool the same way would need: a bare-stem grant needs the bare name in the worker's permissions.tools and a canonical grant the canonical name, neither covering the other, and the worker's capability_credentials seat pools for the tool are read under that same spelling. Unlike the verbs, the grant is pinned with the run (ADR-105 D1): a reload that changes it reaches the next run, never a running one. A type derived with based_on inherits it unchanged, because in_dispatch is part of the base's locked contract.

name.description: The tool granted (the HCL block label): a native tool's name, or a tool recipe as <vault>/tools/<stem> or its bare stem. Resolved when the type loads, and the resolved tool — not this spelling — is what a run is granted and what a call is dispatched to. This spelling, as written, is the one the dispatch's worker is read under, as a step's capability label is.

config.description: The binding config the dispatch hands the tool — the same object a step that names the tool fills from its own config, checked at load against the tool's config_schema with its config_defaults composed beneath. It is the TYPE's and never the caller's: a session cannot widen it through the tool's input, so web-fetch's allow_domains here is the whole of what a session may fetch, and an empty or absent allow_domains still denies every host. A literal object, fixed when the type loads: nothing is substituted into it. Absent hands the tool no binding config.

observations.description: What work of this type is TOLD about its own subjects, unbidden (ADR-100 D6) — the exact mirror of checkpoints, which is what its work REPORTS. Delivery is a pull verb and push is a policy over it, so this block does not decide what is knowable: it decides whether a run of this type is handed what is already known without having to ask. Both halves are load-bearing and this is the half that reaches a language-model harness, because a model that does not know observations exist will never call the verb. The same declaration has a second home on the capability recipe for an invocation with NO Work Order; the two are SELECTED BETWEEN AND NEVER MERGED, so a Work Order of this type whose type declares nothing gets no push even where the dispatched capability declares a policy of its own — a merge would make the delivered set a function of two files, and an author asking why their run was told something could not tell which one to edit. Omitting the block is the default and is no push: a type that has not asked to be told anything has not asked, and nothing is inferred for it. The subjects it resolves about are the type's own subject blocks. LIVE SINCE WAVE 3 ITEM 4 of PLAN-2026-08-learned-operational-knowledge: a dispatch of a type declaring this block IS pushed what is known about its subjects, rendered per mode into whichever driver runs it — a section of the coding harness's own CLAUDE.md, or a section of the tera-native agent's system prompt. THE TWO BOUNDS ARE LIVE TOO, since Wave 3 item 6: past max_full a render stops being full and becomes summary with the reason stated, the set itself untouched at that step, and past max_summary a summary render delivers what fits — the strongest and most recently held, ordered by confidence and then recency — and REPORTS THE COUNT IT ELIDED. THE TWO COMPOSE, so a full set past both degrades AND elides and each fact is named separately. Neither trims silently, the reason rides on the payload the driver serializes rather than only reaching the operator's log, and the D7 delivery record carries the EFFECTIVE mode with degraded saying the unit had asked for more.

mode.description: Whether the typed body rides along with the claim. summary renders each matched observation's required prose summary (ADR-100 D4) and nothing else — a run that needs structure then calls the observations verb, so ignoring the invitation costs it the body rather than the knowledge. full renders the same set plus each observation's typed body, which is right where a subject's history is small and the extra round trip is not worth its latency. Two values rather than a boolean, because a boolean has no correct default and this axis does: empty means summary. The word mode is the ADR-087 §4 per-axis reserved word — identical field set, differing behaviour — and it collides with subject_kind's continuity mode not at all, because the words are per-axis and the blocks are different. A RENDERER HAS NO EDITORIAL LATITUDE: full delivers exactly what the pull verb would have returned, same set, same fields, same order, and may not summarize, reorder, filter or truncate.

max_summary.description: Bound on a summary render, IN OBSERVATIONS RATHER THAN BYTES. Past it a render delivers what fits and reports the count it elided — it never trims silently, because a delivered set that stops being the resolved set while continuing to look like it is the failure honest degradation exists to prevent. The unit is a count and the reason is that the degradation has to be provable: a byte threshold would depend on how verbose a model happened to be inside the free-prose summary ADR-100 D4 obliges and does not bound, which is a boundary that moves between runs and a test that flakes by construction. Bytes are what actually exhaust a window and are being MEASURED BEFORE THEY ARE LEGISLATED — PRD-018 SC10 records bytes rendered per mode, and a byte ceiling is available later as an additive attribute decided on evidence. The bound is declared HERE and not on the subject_kind: a bound is about the consumer's context window, and a kind knows nothing about its consumers — one consumer can be pushed test/ flakes and machine/ safety claims in the same dispatch, and neither kind can hold a number that is right for it. Must be at least 1: there is no spelling for unbounded, and a bound of zero would render nothing while reading as a limit. THE DEFAULT OF 20 IS A STARTING POINT WITH A STATED BASIS, NOT A MEASUREMENT — a summary is one prose line, so twenty is a prompt section rather than a prompt — and it is revisable on PRD-018 SC10 evidence. It carries a default while a subject_kind's mode does not, under ADR-100 D8's own rule: no-default is reserved for choices where absence is dangerous, and a bound guessed generously costs a large prompt rather than a confident falsehood.

max_full.description: Bound on a full render, in observations. Past it a render STOPS BEING full and degrades to summary with the reason stated; no renderer may truncate, so the bound cannot live in one. Two numbers rather than one because ADR-100 D6 describes two degradations at two magnitudes and a typed body is large where a prose line is not, so one number cannot express both. DECLARING IT BESIDE mode = "summary" IS A LOAD ERROR NAMING BOTH REPAIRS — drop the attribute, or declare mode = "full" if a full render was intended — in the posture a checkpoints payload_schema already takes when phases is empty: an attribute that could never be consulted is an authoring error rather than a value to ignore. Must be at least 1, for max_summary's reason. THE DEFAULT OF 5 IS A STARTING POINT WITH A STATED BASIS, NOT A MEASUREMENT — a typed body is unbounded, so five keeps full honest and makes degradation an ordinary safety valve rather than a rarity nobody has seen fire — and it is revisable on PRD-018 SC10 evidence.

invite_writes.description: Whether a dispatch is INVITED TO RECORD what it learned, in the same payload that tells it what is already known (ADR-100 D6 Amendment 3). Defaults to false, and the default is about two costs rather than one: the block's other attributes govern a context cost, and this one governs a context cost AND a write-volume cost, because a producer that accepts the invitation mints records against the ADR-100 D8 per-author budget. Every other delivery decision in this design is a declared per-work-kind policy rather than a global default, for the same reason — you do not want every dispatch writing. IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE LOOP DOES NOT CLOSE ON ITS OWN: everything needed to store operational knowledge ships and is reachable, the push payload already invites a READ, and until this attribute the only route to a write was harness-specific instruction — which is the dependency PRD-018 set out to remove. D6's argument for push existing at all is that a model that does not know observations exist will never call the verb, and that is exactly as true of the write verb. A BOOLEAN, AND THE SCOPE IS NOT THE AUTHOR'S TO DECLARE: it does not say what to invite writes about because that was declared one block over — push resolves about the dispatch's own subject blocks and the invitation is over exactly that set, naming those subjects and nothing else. THE SENTENCE A RUN READS IS THE DAEMON'S AND IS NOT AUTHORABLE. There is deliberately no free-text half: a guidance string would be a second authority on what the run was told, one per recipe rather than one per harness; it could not be validated, so an authoring mistake would surface as a producer behaving oddly months later; and it would put per-deployment prompt engineering into a config file. A driver decides only where the sentence lands and in what markup, which is the split D6 Amendment 1 already rules for the degradation notice. AN INVITED DISPATCH IS INVITED EVEN WHEN NOTHING IS KNOWN YET — the run with nothing to be told is precisely the run that may have something to record, and every subject's first observation comes from a dispatch in exactly that state, so a delivery carrying the invitation and no claims is a real delivery. The four not-pushed reasons are unaffected: a refusal is not an invitation, and a dispatch that resolves no subjects has nothing for one to be about.

history.description: What a SETTLED TRAIN of this type is worth after it ends (ADR-145 D7): how long it stays in the hot store, and what is archived before it leaves. One question with a when (window) and a what (archive), so it is one block - a recipe cannot declare half of it. Once the window has passed, every member of the train stays behind as a STUB, its own Work Order row thinned to its final state, which get, tree and depends_on still answer and list returns when asked with include_archived; the train's events, results and other history rows are deleted, after its record is sealed into the archive when archive asks for one. A train leaves no earlier than its window and can leave later: a live row naming a member (a parked run, a seat lease, a subject claim) holds it and is reported, and an artifact or step binding of the train holds it until that store's own window has passed. A STUB IS READ-ONLY: every mutating verb on it is refused as archived, so a cancelled train can no longer be force-failed and retried once it is trimmed - the window is its recovery period. OMITTING THE BLOCK IS KEEP-ALL: a train of a type that declares nothing is never trimmed, and no default window applies to it anywhere (ADR-145 Open 1). Declare the block on a type whose settled trains may leave the hot store after the window - a periodic sweep or a janitor tick with archive = none, or an audit-bound type with archive = full or failures, whose record work_order.history reads back.

window.description: How long a settled train of this type stays in the hot store, as a Go duration string (72h is three days), measured from the train's LAST terminal transition - a train that is retried and settles again starts its window again (ADR-145 D3). The type owns the value within a deployment ceiling, which is ADR-114 D5's resolution for activity_partition.retention.window reused with its attribute name and its numbers. Omitting it takes the deployment default for the resolved deployment_profile - 7 days for embedded, desktop, dev and test; 30 days for server and gateway. A window above the 365-day ceiling is CLAMPED to it rather than refused, and the daemon log reports the clamp once per type. The sweep runs hourly, so a train leaves somewhere between its window and its window plus an hour. A window BELOW THE 24h FLOOR IS REFUSED at load: the floor keeps a cursor consumer that was offline overnight reconcilable from the hot store and keeps yesterday's failure findable. SET THE WINDOW WELL ABOVE THE LONGEST WORKSPACE ttl of any volume binding this type declares - about 30 days is the normal value, and the 24h floor is a platform minimum, not a recommendation. A train trimmed while its workspace is still retained cannot be resumed onto it; its stub keeps the workspace locator and the volume's own ttl still reclaims the bytes, but the session is lost. This is guidance and is not checked at load.

archive.description: Which trains are written to the archive before the trim. REQUIRED, with no default: whether a type's record is kept is stated by whoever declares the block, never assumed (ADR-145 Open 1). full archives every train. failures archives a train in which any member ended failed or ever entered failed:awaiting-ack - a retried failure counts even when the train later completed - and drops the rest; cancelled does not count, because a cancel is an intentional removal, and neither does superseded, but a cancelled member later force-failed counts from then on. none archives no train - the stub left behind records the train as dropped, and its events, results and other rows are gone. A train that needs a record is sealed into the archive and read back before any of its rows are deleted; while the archive cannot take or verify a record, that train stays in the hot store, and trains that need none are still trimmed. A kept record is read back whole by work_order.history (tera workorder history <id>); a dropped train answers that read with the dropped refusal, never with an empty record.

sandbox.description: What this type says about the sandbox of EVERY DISPATCH it makes (ADR-069 D12), spelled as a tool recipe's sandbox block is because it speaks to the same axis. It is INTERSECTED with the tool's posture and never replaces it, so a type can narrow a sandbox and cannot widen one. The type is the home because only the work knows what it reads: the tool's ceiling is chosen by the tool's vault and its allow-list serves every type the tool runs for, so a type whose sessions read untrusted text beside private material has no other way to close the hosts that text could steer them to. PINNED WITH THE RUN (ADR-105 D1): removing the block changes what runs next and never widens a run already pinned. Omitting it leaves every dispatch on the tool's own posture, byte for byte as before the block existed.

network.description: connections gives every dispatch of this type NO NETWORK EXCEPT ITS CONNECTIONS' PROXY ROUTES. The tool's allow-list is not consulted and its outbound proxy is not started: the sandbox may reach only the loopback ports and the socket of the dispatch's injecting proxy (ADR-148 D4), which darwin's kernel sandbox holds it to. That proxy DROPS EVERY CREDENTIAL HEADER THE SESSION SENDS - Authorization, x-api-key, api-key, x-goog-api-key and every header a connection names - before it presents the deployment's, so a model host is reached only with the deployment's credential and an attacker's key planted in the session buys nothing. A harness therefore reaches its model only through a connection its toolchain routes. A pairing with a tool that needs network and routes nothing through a connection is REFUSED at load and at tera config plan, naming the tool: codex is such a tool today, because its model credential is delivered into the sandbox rather than through a proxy. A tool that asks for no network loses nothing and runs. Omitting it keeps the tool's own posture.

timeout.description: How much working time every dispatch of this type may have (Go duration, e.g. 45m or 2h): its capability, each select candidate and each capability step of its workflow. It is the tool recipe's sandbox.timeout in the same words and the same duration rule, and it must be positive. IT ONLY NARROWS: a dispatch runs for the least of this value, the tool recipe's sandbox.timeout and the tool's ceiling (the policy profile, and for a plugin tool its installation's approved wallclock), so the tool's own timeout is the upper limit. A value above the maximum of a tool the type dispatches is REFUSED by tera config validate, tera config plan and the apply gate, naming both values and where the maximum comes from; a run pinned before its maximum was lowered runs at the new maximum and logs WARN tool sandbox_timeout_narrowed. Like the tool's timeout it is measured on the monotonic clock of the host running the dispatch, so time that host spends asleep does not count against it. It is pinned with the Work Order, so an edit changes what runs next and never what is already running. Empty, which is what a parameter defaulting to an empty string writes, keeps the tool's own timeout, as does omitting it.
